items.caption: CHESS NOTATION is as useful as the alphabet, and much easier to learn. It is the magic key that opens the door to the entire wealth of chess literature. By its use you can play over the exciting games of the masters for sheer pleasure, or study their comments on the various moves to improve your own playing ability. Notation is simply a brief way of describing what happens on the chessboard – where the pieces move, or what captures they make. These are the initial letters and symbols for the pieces:

The pieces set up at the beginning of a game. The bottom row from left to right is the first rank. The White Pawns stand on the second rank. The row above the second rank is the third rank, and so on to the last row, which is the eighth rank.
Position after 1 e4.
Position after Black’s third move. Note that Black has two Pawns on the e-file. In switching to the e-file, Black’s d-Pawn now becomes an e-Pawn.

Black’s Queen gave check on the 6th move and then captured the White Pawn on e5. Black is now threatening to take the opponent’s knight on e4. But White’s next move, Queen-side castling, sets a deadly trap.
White forces a mate in three moves, beginning with a beautiful Queen sacrifice.
White checks the Black King, and at the same time he attacks Black’s Rook. The King must move out of check, the Rook is captured next move. This is an example of double attack.
White attacks the weak c-Pawn five times; it is defended only four times. The Pawn cannot be saved. This is an example of concentration of superior force.

3A. White moves. He has taken advantage of the vulnerable position of the two Black pieces placed in a straight line. How? His Rook pins the Black Knight, which must not move because of the resulting loss of Black’s Rook. How can White increase the pressure in order to exploit Black’s predicament? The indicated answer is: attack the Knight again! Therefore: 1 f4! See Diagram 3B.

Casting about desperately for some resource, he notes that Black’s King and Queen are placed on the same straight line, but that a Black Pawn blocks any chance of a pin by g1. Therefore, he removes the Pawn: 1 xg7+!! See Diagram 4B.

items.caption: 3B. Black moves. His Knight is now menaced by two pieces, defended by only one. The Knight is lost, and will be captured by White on the following move.

items.caption: 55A. White moves. He begins with 1 c6, attacking the Rook at Black’s d8. Relatively best is 1 ... xc6, losing “only” the exchange. But suppose Black is stubborn and tries to save the Rook? Then we get 1 ... e8; 2 e7+! with a “family check” on Black’s King, Queen and Rook! A remarkable concentration of force.

items.caption: 54B. White moves. He naturally plays 2 xc7. Then comes the expected Knight fork 2 ... e2+, and after 3 h1, xc1 Black is a whole Rook to the good.

items.caption: 68A. Black moves. His target is the f-Pawn – although it is defended by three pieces! He begins with a capture, 1 ... xe5, enabling him to foresee White’s reply, 2 xe5. Now the vulnerable point has only two defenders – one of them pinned! But how does the Knight fork materialize?!

items.caption: 67B. White moves. He is helpless: the Knight forks his King and Queen, and the White c-Pawn, being pinned, is unable to capture the intruder! “A pinned piece is a paralyzed piece.” So White must move his King, allowing his Queen to be captured. A subtle example of this theme.
items.label: 67B

items.caption: 68B. Black moves. He strikes at once: a violent move is required, before the defense can be reinforced. The solution: 2 ... xf2+! As White’s Rook is pinned, he is limited to 3 xf2 (allowing 3 ... d3+); or 3 e1 (again allowing 3 ... d3+); or 3 g1 (allowing 3 ... xg2 mate). The fork and pin worked hand in glove!
items.label: 68B

items.caption: 69A. White moves. He wins by a neat combination involving two successive Knight forks followed by a capture based on a pin. In actual play, this is easier done than said! White begins with 1 xc6, a Knight fork threatening Queen and Bishop. This forces 1 ... c7, and now comes the astonishing fork 2 e7+ attacking King and Rook.
items.label: 69A

Black defends with 2 ... f8 (only one Rook can go to this square – which Rook?). Now 3 g5 again adds to the pressure. Black will be unable to withstand the hammering on his pinned Rook.
items.label: 71A

items.caption: 69B. Black moves. He plays 2 ... xe7 (else 3 xf5 winning the exchange). Now comes 3 xf5! with a simple and familiar pinning position. Whether White succumbs to 3 ... exf5; 4 xe7 or not, he is the exchange down. Picture 69A without the Knight at e5, and the capture xf5 immediately strikes your eye. White forced this position with no loss of time.
items.label: 69B

items.label: 70B

items.label: 112B

items.caption: 112B. Black moves. Now he has the position he wanted. He must “discover” an attack on the Queen at once, so that she cannot escape. Only one move will answer that requirement: 2 ... xh2+ attacking the White King with the Bishop, and attacking the White Queen with the Rook! White must reply 3 xh2, whereupon 3 ... xd3 wins. Q.E.D.
items.label: 112B

items.caption: 113B. White moves. He must get out of check, permitting the loss of his Queen by 3 ... xd3. We are becoming familiar with the basic pattern for the discovered attack. The Black Bishop masked a possible attack on White’s Queen. Therefore we moved the Bishop with check, unmasking the Rook’s attack on White’s helpless Queen. Remember the priority of check!
items.label: 113B

items.caption: 114A. White moves. One of the most dangerous features of the discovered attack is that it is often a concealed weapon. In the diagram, for example, White’s Queen has enormous power on the c-file, even though its action is masked by the White Bishop. There follows 1 xc7!, threatening to remove the Black Rook. Black naturally answers 1 ... xc7.
items.label: 114A

items.caption: 115A. White moves. Here his problem is the correct sequence of his moves. There is a potential attack via the d-file, but how is White’s Bishop to leave d4 in order to unmask an attack by the Rook? 1 xb6?? is a gross blunder because of 1 ... xb6+. 1 xg7+, xg7; 2 xd7 is much better, but wins only a Pawn. The correct sequence begins with 1 xd7!, which must be answered by 1 ... xd7.
items.label: 115A

items.caption: 116A. White moves. He has just sacrificed a Rook, relying on the basic pattern for a discovered attack which is now available. The position on the first rank is suggestive: White’s Bishop is obviously going to unmask an attack on the Black Queen. But how, with Black’s King on a white square?! White cuts the Gordian knot: 1 xf8+! Black replies 1 ... xf8.
items.label: 116A

items.caption: 115B. White moves. Black has been given no option. That is the first good point about the proper order of moves. The second valuable feature is that the Black target has been transformed from a Knight into the immensely valuable Queen. Now comes 2 xg7+, “discovering” a Rook attack on Black’s Queen, which is lost next move. Also feasible is 2 xb6, winning a piece by “dis covery.”
items.label: 115B

items.caption: 115B. White moves. Black has been given no option. That is the first good point about the proper order of moves. The second valuable feature is that the Black target has been transformed from a Knight into the immensely valuable Queen. Now comes 2 xg7+, “discovering” a Rook attack on Black’s Queen, which is lost next move. Also feasible is 2 xb6, winning a piece by “dis covery.”
items.label: 115B

items.caption: 116B. White moves. Now that Black’s King is on a black square, White continues 2 h6+ winning the Queen, as Black must get out of check. With a Pawn ahead, White wins easily. Suppose that after 1 xf8+, Black had replied 1 ... d7. There would still be a “discovery” pattern after 2 d6+, e8; 3 g5! threatening mate!
items.label: 116B

items.caption: 117A. White moves. This diagram illustrates a basic idea which occurs innumerable times. To understand and apply this idea, you need only understand the pattern for discovered attack: White’s Queen is a potential threat to any piece on the d-file, even though momentarily masked by the Bishop.
items.label: 117A

items.caption: 118A. Black moves. The possibility of a discovered attack is obscured here; but when you know the pattern, you know what to look for. The decisive clue is the fact that White’s Queen is not protected. Black begins with a Knight fork sacrifice: 1 ... f3+. White’s Rook is attacked, so he plays 2 gxf3. Now 2 ... g6+ forces 3 h1. The pattern for a discovered attack is established!
items.label: 118A

items.caption: 119A. White moves. White’s Bishop seems to have but little scope, yet it is easy to imagine a situation in which the Bishop attacks through the medium of a forceful utilization of the Knight. The problem is to make a possible Knight check practical. The doubled Rooks give us a point of departure:
items.label: 119A

items.caption: 118B. Black moves. His Queen is now on the same diagonal as the adverse Queen – separated only by a Black Knight; a perfect setting for a discovered attack. Black plays 3 ... g3+, forcing White to do something about the check. Consequently White has no time to save his defenseless Queen. Had White’s Queen been protected, the combination would have been impossible.
items.label: 118B

items.caption: 118B. Black moves. His Queen is now on the same diagonal as the adverse Queen – separated only by a Black Knight; a perfect setting for a discovered attack. Black plays 3 ... g3+, forcing White to do something about the check. Consequently White has no time to save his defenseless Queen. Had White’s Queen been protected, the combination would have been impossible.
items.label: 118B

items.caption: 120A. Black moves. He sees a familiar pattern in the position of the two Queens, with the Knight between them. What move can the Knight make which will be a “smite” while at the same time exposing White’s Queen to attack? Black has no check and no mate threat, but he does have a capture: 1 ... xe4!
items.label: 120A

items.caption: 120A. Black moves. He sees a familiar pattern in the position of the two Queens, with the Knight between them. What move can the Knight make which will be a “smite” while at the same time exposing White’s Queen to attack? Black has no check and no mate threat, but he does have a capture: 1 ... xe4!
items.label: 120A

items.caption: 121A. Black moves. He produces a drastic example of the crushing power of the discovered attack. The key idea is to move his Rook from f3, unmasking an attack by his Bishop on White’s Queen. To create the most havoc, he combines this “discovery” with a capture: 1 ... xd3! Note that White’s Queen is now pinned and cannot guard the Rook at d1!
items.label: 121A

items.caption: 122A. White moves. Both his Bishops mask a possible attack by his Rook on Black’s Queen. To bring about a discovered attack along the d-file, it is necessary to move the Bishops. First comes a threat: 1 c4, attacking Black’s Rook on a2. Black replies 1 ... a8. Now we have gained time to devise the proper setting for the discovered attack.
items.label: 122A

items.caption: 120B. White moves. He is in a terrible predicament! He cannot capture the Knight, for his Queen is en prise. Nor can he merely move his Queen out of the line of attack, for then 2 ... xd2+ will win both Rooks. White must submit to playing 2 xe5, xd2+! (this interpolation is vital!) followed by 3 ... xe5.
items.label: 120B

items.caption: 121B. White moves. He is threatened with 2 ... xd1 mate. If he plays 2 xd3, then comes 2 ... e1 mate (remember the Queen is pinned!). White therefore tries 2 xa8, hoping for 2 ... xa8?; 3 xd3 etc. But, utilizing the priority of check (as in 120B) Black plays 2 ... xd1+! first, confiscating White’s Queen later on, and remaining a Rook and Bishop ahead.
items.label: 121B

items.caption: 123A. Black moves. By moving his Bishop, he can uncover an attack on White’s Knight. The Bishop cannot check, capture or threaten mate. What forceful possibility remains?! He can attack! Therefore: 1 ... h3. Black’s Queen attacks the Knight; Black’s Bishop attacks the Rook.
items.label: 123A

items.caption: 123A. Black moves. By moving his Bishop, he can uncover an attack on White’s Knight. The Bishop cannot check, capture or threaten mate. What forceful possibility remains?! He can attack! Therefore: 1 ... h3. Black’s Queen attacks the Knight; Black’s Bishop attacks the Rook.
items.label: 123A

items.caption: 125A. White moves. A discovered attack is indicated on the c-file. But there is a difficulty to be ironed out: White’s Queen is en prise!
items.label: 125A

items.caption: 123B. White moves. He must lose some material, as both Knight and Rook are menaced. His “best” course is to save his Knight, allowing the loss of the exchange.
items.label: 123B

items.caption: 124B. White moves. By advancing, the Black Pawn has attacked the Queen, simultaneously opening up the diagonal of his King’s Bishop for an attack on White’s unguarded Bishop on a3.
items.label: 124B

items.caption: 125B. White moves. He continues with the pretty move 2 b5, discovering attack on Black’s Queen by the White Rook, and at the same time forking Black’s Queen and Rook with the Knight. Black must move his Queen (obviously 2 ... axb5? is out of the question); and after 3 xd4, White winds up the exchange ahead. The double threat was too potent to be parried.
items.label: 125B

items.caption: 126A. Black moves. The position on the c-file calls for a discovered attack on White’s Queen by a move of Black’s Bishop.
items.label: 126A

items.caption: 126A. Black moves. The position on the c-file calls for a discovered attack on White’s Queen by a move of Black’s Bishop.
items.label: 126A

items.caption: 126B. White moves. Black has “discovered” an attack on White’s Queen; at the same time the unmasking Bishop creates the terrible threat ... xh2 mate. White must lose at least a piece (3 c4, xc4).
items.label: 126B

items.caption: 127A. White moves. He begins by driving the Black Rook at f8 into position for the discovered attack pattern: 1 e7. Black replies 1 ... e8. Now 2 b4 threatens 3 xe8 mate, or 3 xb4.
items.label: 127A

items.caption: 128. White moves. By what discovered attack does he win the Queen?
128. White moves. By what discovered attack does he win the Queen?
129. White moves. By what discovered attack does he win a piece?
130. Black moves. By what discovered attack does he win the Queen?

132. White moves. He will give the discovered check on the e-file. In the diagram, Black’s King is screened from check by the White Knight. Any move of the Knight will keep Black’s King busy getting out of check from the unmasked White Rook.

133A. White moves. His seventh rank forms the basic pattern for a discovered check: any move by the Bishop will discover a check by White’s Rook. The problem is to find a target for the white-squared Bishop. This is done by forcing the Knight to a white square: 1 b4!
items.label: 133A

items.caption: 133A. White moves. His seventh rank forms the basic pattern for a discovered check: any move by the Bishop will discover a check by White’s Rook. The problem is to find a target for the white-squared Bishop. This is done by forcing the Knight to a white square: 1 b4!
items.label: 133A

items.caption: 133B. Black moves. His Knight is lost! 1 ... b7? or 1 ... b3? is out of the question. 1 ... c4 is answered by 2 xc4+ leaving Black no time to capture (remember the priority of check!). So Black tries 1 ... c6, but 2 d5+ wins the piece.
items.label: 133B

items.caption: 134A. White moves. He begins with a startling sacrifice: 1 f7! forks Black’s Queen and Rook. After 1 ... xf7 the f-file forms the pattern for a discovered check: 2 fxg5+. Now we see the point of the diabolical first move.
items.label: 134A

items.caption: 134B. Black moves. His King has been lured into occupying the same file as White’s Rook. The f-Pawn opens the way for the Rook’s gunfire and stabs at the Black Queen. However Black may play, his Queen is lost.
items.label: 134B

items.caption: 135A. Black moves. Any Rook move by Black will subject his opponent to check while the Rook tries to gobble up material. The most forceful way is 1 ... xa2+; 2 g1, g2+; but after 3 h1, what has White gained?!
items.label: 135A

items.caption: 135B. Black moves. He has altered the position slightly but decisively. The pattern for discovered check remains, but in a more deadly form: White’s Bishop is no longer supported by a Pawn! Now comes 3 ... b2+; 4 g1, xb3.
items.label: 135B

items.caption: 136A. Black moves. By removing the extraneous factors in complicated positions, you produce the design for winning; thus the “brilliant” 1 ... xg3! forces 2 fxg3. What has Black achieved by the sacrifice? How will he turn it to account? By means of a discovered check.
items.label: 136A

items.caption: 136B. Black moves. By sacrificing his Queen, he forced the opening of the diagonal between Black’s Bishop and White’s King, creating the basic pattern for a discovered check. White’s Queen is the biggest prey in sight, so Black pounces on it with 2 ... d1+.
items.label: 136B

items.caption: 137A. White moves. He plays 1 d7+ (double attack), when 1 ... c7 is compulsory. Now 2 xc7+, xc7 and we have the basic pattern for discovered check on the c-file. So: 3 f8+!
items.label: 137A

items.caption: 137B. Black moves. His Bishop is attacked, but cannot be saved. The Black King has been put in check by White’s double-duty Bishop. Once the King moves out of check, White plays 4 xg7, winning easily.
items.label: 137B

items.caption: 138A. White moves. His first move is a simple method of forcing a position which he has already pictured in his mind. The image derives from the basic pattern for discovered check:
items.label: 138A

items.caption: 139. White moves. How does he win the Queen by a discovered check?
139. White moves. How does he win the Queen by a discovered check?
140. White moves. How does he win the Queen by a discovered check?

142. Black moves. He ignores the fact that his Queen is en prise, for he notes that his Queen is in line with the hostile King, separated only by a piece which can also give check. This is the basic pattern for double check. Black plays 1 ... f3+, giving checkmate on the move. White cannot capture, he cannot interpose, he cannot move his King.

142. Black moves. He ignores the fact that his Queen is en prise, for he notes that his Queen is in line with the hostile King, separated only by a piece which can also give check. This is the basic pattern for double check. Black plays 1 ... f3+, giving checkmate on the move. White cannot capture, he cannot interpose, he cannot move his King.

143A. White moves. He begins by examining possible captures and checks. 1 xg6 leads to nothing, so he turns to 1 g5+, noting that Black can reply 1 ... xf7. Can reply?! – no: must reply! This excites White’s interest, for he sees that he can force Black into a double check. The play goes: 1 g5+!, xf7; and now we have the pattern for a double check.
items.label: 143A

items.caption: 144A. Black moves. The mighty Bishop on the “long diagonal” leading to White’s King is the star actor here. But the diagonal is momentarily blocked by a White Pawn. To suggest the obstacle is to remove it: 1 ... xf3! Black surrenders his Queen in order to achieve the basic pattern for a double check. There follows 2 xe2, xf1 mate!
items.label: 144A

items.caption: 145A. White moves. The position of his Rook on the g-file gives him an idea for constructing the basic pattern for a double check. The g-file is now half open; do you see how it can be forced open all the way against Black’s vulnerable King? The answer: 1 xh5!, gxh5; 2 xe6+.
items.label: 145A

items.caption: 143B. White moves. He completes the combination with 2 d6 mate! This drastic finish bears out the deadly reputation of the double check: the Knight cannot be captured because of the Queen check, and interposition is impossible because of the Knight check! All that remains is self-help: move the King. But all exits are blocked. The King is checkmated.
items.label: 143B

items.caption: 145B. Black moves. His King is doubly checked, and must move. The impudent Knight is therefore immune. After Black’s King moves, there follows 3 xc7 and White has won a piece.
items.label: 145B

items.caption: 146. Black moves. If he plays 1 ... xg4, how does White win at once?
146. Black moves. If he plays 1 ... xg4, how does White win at once?

148. Black moves. His Queen attacks a Rook, his Knight attacks the Bishop. The Knight at d2 serves no defensive purpose, being pinned and therefore paralyzed. Hence White’s Queen must guard the menaced pieces. To prove that the Queen is overworked, Black plays 1 ... xf3+. After 2 xf3 White’s Queen no longer guards the Rook, so that 2 ... xb1+ wins.
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 148. Black moves. His Queen attacks a Rook, his Knight attacks the Bishop. The Knight at d2 serves no defensive purpose, being pinned and therefore paralyzed. Hence White’s Queen must guard the menaced pieces. To prove that the Queen is overworked, Black plays 1 ... xf3+. After 2 xf3 White’s Queen no longer guards the Rook, so that 2 ... xb1+ wins.
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 149A. White moves. Searching for a weakness in Black’s position, he spots it in Black’s e-Pawn. This Pawn guards the Knight at d6 (which is attacked by a White Bishop) and also the Bishop at f6 (which is attacked by a White Rook). Thus the e-Pawn has a double task; it is overworked; it can be undermined. The most logical course is 1 xd6 forcing 1 ... exd6.
items.label: 149A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 150A. White moves. Black’s pieces seem amply protected, but the fact that they are mutually dependent on each other for support is thoughtprovoking. The overworked motif may be present! Sure enough, the Rook at h8 guards both Rook and Bishop, which are both attacked by the Rook at g7. The Rook at h8 is therefore overworked. There follows 1 xh7!
items.label: 150A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 151A. Black moves. He wants to play ... e2, threatening ... xh2 mate or ... g2 mate. At first sight ... e2 seems impossible, as the square in question is guarded by White’s Rook at e1. But this Rook also has to guard the Rook at f1, and is therefore an overworked piece! We undermine it with 1 ... e2!
items.label: 151A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 149B. White moves. The overworked e-Pawn has now been displaced, no longer defending the Bishop. So White continues 2 xf6, with a piece to the good. (Sometimes there is more than one way of undermining a piece. For example, White could have played 1 xf6, exf6; 2 xd6 with two pieces for a Rook. But 1 xd6 is even stronger.)
items.label: 149B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 151B. White moves. He is menaced by two different mates on the second rank, and the only plausible defense 2 xe2 allows 2 ... xf1 mate in reply. In Diagram 151B, White’s Rook at e1 is an overworked piece; it cannot defend against every threat. The brilliant 1 ... e2! is easy to see once we realize that the overworked piece must be undermined.
items.label: 151B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 151B. White moves. He is menaced by two different mates on the second rank, and the only plausible defense 2 xe2 allows 2 ... xf1 mate in reply. In Diagram 151B, White’s Rook at e1 is an overworked piece; it cannot defend against every threat. The brilliant 1 ... e2! is easy to see once we realize that the overworked piece must be undermined.
items.label: 151B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 152A. White moves. There are Knight forks in the air! Following the maxim that one must look at every check and capture, White studies 1 xb7 forking Queen and Rook. Then he notices 1 xe6+ forking King and Queen. But in each case, the fork is guarded by Black’s Bishop. In each case?! That is our clue! We play 1 xb7!
items.label: 152A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 153A. White moves. His first impulse is to move away his Queen from attack. But note this: the Bishop which is doing the attacking is guarded by Black’s Queen. But the other Black Bishop at e7 is also protected by the Queen from capture by White’s Rook. Doesn’t that make Black’s Queen an overworked piece? And if so, shouldn’t White do something about it, instead of meekly retreating? He plays 1 xe7!
items.label: 153A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 154A. Black moves. He sees that White’s pinned Knight is protected by King and Queen – two pieces – and attacked by two pieces. He also sees that White’s Bishop is protected by the Queen. In other words, the protection of the Queen is common to both the Knight and Bishop. To undermine the overworked Queen, Black plays 1 ... xd2+. White re plies 2 xd2.
items.label: 154A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 153B. Black moves. His attack on the Queen has become meaningless, as 1 ... xf3 is answered by 2 xd7, and White has gained a piece.
items.label: 153B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 154B. Black moves. White’s Queen has been diverted from the protection of the Bishop, so that Black can now wind up with the killing 2 ... xf3+, forking King and Queen.
items.label: 154B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 155A. White moves. Black’s game looks solid, but it has weaknesses. The weak chink in his armor is the Bishop at f6, which has to be guarded by Black’s Queen; Black’s g-Pawn, being pinned, has no defensive value. But Black’s Queen also has to guard the Bishop at b7, so our problem boils down to this: how can we harry the Queen? Answer: 1 e4!
items.label: 155A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 155A. White moves. Black’s game looks solid, but it has weaknesses. The weak chink in his armor is the Bishop at f6, which has to be guarded by Black’s Queen; Black’s g-Pawn, being pinned, has no defensive value. But Black’s Queen also has to guard the Bishop at b7, so our problem boils down to this: how can we harry the Queen? Answer: 1 e4!
items.label: 155A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 156A. White moves. Once we spot the overworked piece, the method of undermining it is as delightful as it is logical. In this case it is the Black Rook at f8 which is overworked, improbable as it may seem. This Rook has the duty of guarding the Queen and the other Rook at h8. The undermining process begins with 1 d8+!
items.label: 156A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 157A. White moves. Is Black’s Queen overworked? The Queen protects the Rook and also prevents mate at Black’s g7. Yet the Queen is not overworked, as after 1 xg5, xg5 the mate is still guarded. To convert the Queen into an overworked piece, it is necessary to shift the scene of the exchange of Rooks. This is done by 1 h4+.
items.label: 157A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 155B. Black moves. If he plays 1 ... xe4, then 2 xf6+ forks King and Queen. Hence Black tries 1 ... c7 but loses a piece after 2 xb7, xb7; 3 xf6+ etc. (The pinned state of the g-Pawn is crucial!) 1 e4! is an ideal example of undermining an overworked piece, as the Queen can no longer guard both Bishops. Maxim: Disturb the overworked piece!
items.label: 155B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 156B. Black moves. He is in check, and he realizes that the checking move will draw the Rook away from f8, so that one of the guarded pieces will lose its protection. Thus if 1 ... xd8; 2 xf4 wins the Queen. Or if 1 ... c7; 2 xf4, xf4; 3 xh8 with an easy win. Rarely has an overworked piece been undermined so artistically.
items.label: 156B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 157B. Black moves. He finds that the check is not easy to answer: if 1 ... g8; 2 e7+ forks King and Queen. He therefore interposes: 1 ... h5. But now the scene of the exchange has been shifted. The Queen must stand guard over two unrelated points and thus becomes an overworked piece. The proof: 2 xh5+, xh5; 3 xg7 mate.
items.label: 157B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 158A. White moves. Black’s Rook at h8 is chained to his post to prevent xh7 mate. Consequently the Rook may become an overworked piece. If it is given another duty, it will crack under the strain! White plays 1 f8!, relying on the fact that 1 ... xf8? would permit 2 xh7 mate. Black’s best chance is to give up the exchange, but let us suppose he tries 1 ... e8.
items.label: 158A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 159A. White moves. He sees that the Black Queen is overworked: it has the double duty of guarding the f-Pawn and the Rook at c6. A capture by White will undermine the overworked piece – but what is the right capture? 1 xc6?, xc6 brings the Rook at a7 to the defense of the f-Pawn. So we try reverse English: 1 xf7+!
items.label: 159A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 160A. White moves. The play pivots on the fact that Black’s Queen is overworked: she defends the b-Pawn and also prevents f8 mate. White fastens on this weakness by playing 1 xb7! As 1 ... xb7? permits 2 f8 mate, Black has nothing better than 1 ... c7. Now his Rook at d8 guards the mate on the last rank.
items.label: 160A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 159B. Black moves. He must play 1 ... xf7 (if 1 ... h8??; 2 g8 mate). Now comes 2 xf7+, (or )xf7; 3 xc6. White’s combination has won the exchange and a Pawn.
items.label: 159B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 160B. White moves. True, the mate on the back rank is stopped, but White is merciless: he spots a newly created weakness in Black’s camp. Black’s Queen is still overworked, guarding the Knight at c7 and also parrying the threat of f6+, made possible by the removal of the Knight to c7. So: 2 xc7!, xc7; 3 f6+ forcing mate!
items.label: 160B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR UNDERMINING THE OVERWORKED PIECE

items.caption: 161. Black moves. White’s Rook at c1 guards the other White Rook and the Bishop as well. What capture undermines the overworked piece?
161. Black moves. White’s Rook at c1 guards the other White Rook and the Bishop as well. What capture undermines the overworked piece?
162. Black moves. White’s Queen prevents mate at g2 and also guards the Knight at d3. What capture demonstrates that the White Queen is overworked?
163. White moves. Black’s Knight at c6 defends two pieces. How does White prove that this Knight is overworked?

165. White moves. Black’s King is tied down to the defense of his Queen. If the King can be forced away, the Queen will be lost. The most forceful move is always a check or a capture. White plays 1 g7+! forcing the removal of the piece guarding the Queen. Black must play 1 ... xg7, whereupon 2 xe7+ is decisive.

items.caption: 166A. White moves. He sees that the vulnerable point in Black’s game is the Rook on d5, guarded only by the Black Queen. With White’s Queen and both Black Rooks in line, thoughts of a double attack suggest themselves. The guard must be removed! Therefore: 1 e7! This forces Black to abandon the protection of the Rook, with the continuation 1 ... xe7; 2 xd5+.

items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 170A. Black moves. His pin on the Knight would normally yield dividends by the application of more pressure – say by ... e6. But he has no time, as his own Bishop is attacked. But there is a quicker course. The unhappy Knight is protected only by pieces. Therefore Black removes one of the guards with 1 ... xg2+.
items.label: 170A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 171A. White moves. He has an open file for his King’s Rook, and simple doubling on this file would suffice to win (1 h5, g6; 2 ah1 etc.). But there is a quicker, more dynamic way, based on the fact that Black’s defensive force is scattered: 1 h7+! The Rook must be captured (if 1 ... g8? or 1 ... g6?; 2 xf7 mate).
items.label: 171A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 169B. Black moves. To save his Queen he must play 1 ... xg4. Now White does not continue 2 fxg4? (which leaves him a Rook down after 2 ... xe1). Instead he continues as planned: 2 xe8+, now that the Rook’s defender has been removed. Black has no time to save his Queen (priority of check!). After 2 ... g7; 3 fxg4 wins easily.
items.label: 169B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 170B. White moves. His reply is forced: 2 xg2. Now that White’s Knight has lost a vital prop, Black has a winning double attack: 2 ... xe4+ (2 ... xe4+ is also good); 3 xe4, xe4+ followed by 4 ... xb1. An inventory of the final position shows Black to be a piece ahead, with an easy win. The winning method here is of great practical value.
items.label: 170B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 171B. Black moves. As we have shown, 1 ... xh7 is forced. But now White has removed the only defender (the Black King!) of the f-Pawn, or, more exactly, of the square f7. After 2 xf7+, Black has 2 ... h8 or 2 ... h6; in either event 3 h1+ puts Black out of his misery. In this case, removing the guard led to a mating attack.
items.label: 171B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 172A. White moves. He attacks the hostile Knight twice. It is defended twice. Both guards are pieces. If either defender can be captured or driven off, the Knight will be lost – his guard will be removed. These reflections lead logically to 1 b6, which forks both guards: the Rook and Bishop.
items.label: 172A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 173A. Black moves. His Rook attacks White’s Knight, which is defended by a Bishop. Remove this guard and White’s position collapses. As in 172A, a Knight fork does the trick: 1 ... c4. The menaced Rook must stay on the second rank to guard the Bishop, hence 2 c2. Black is well on the way to achieving his objective.
items.label: 173A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 174A. White moves. He sees that the position of the hostile Knight is shaky. It has two defenders – but both can be knocked out. How? Not by 1 xd6?, cxd6; 2 dxe5, dxe5 and the Knight is guarded by a sturdy Pawn. We need a more accurate order of moves: 1 dxe5!, xe5 (if 1 ... xe5; 2 xf4 wins a piece). Now to remove a guard.
items.label: 174A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 172B. Black moves. He plays 1 ... b8. This is inadequate, but he has nothing better. Now there follows 2 xa8, xa8 and, amusingly enough, neither of the Black Knight’s guards is functioning. White now captures the Knight, with a piece ahead. Maxim: Knock out the prop, and the piece falls!
items.label: 172B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 173B. Black moves. Has he really come nearer to his goal? He has blocked the action of his own Rook, and even permitted White to increase the Knight’s protection. But, as has been pointed out, pieces are unstable guards. Now comes 2 ... xb2; 3 xb2. Both defenders are gone; 3 ... xc3 wins the piece after all. An impressive example because of its simplicity.
items.label: 173B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 174B. White moves. With the Knight guarded by two pieces, the rest is easy: remove one of the guards. The move we want is 2 xd6, and whichever way Black recaptures, we continue with 3 xf4. The way in which White proves that the Knight is inadequately defended is genuinely instructive.
items.label: 174B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 175A. White moves. His attack is concentrated against the pinned Knight. He can remove the guard (the King) by 1 h8+, but after 1 ... xh8; 2 xg6 he has lost material: the Knight is less valuable than the sacrificed Rook. But try a different order of moves: 1 xg6+ xg6.
items.label: 175A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 176A. White moves. Our familiarity with removing the guard suggests that Black’s Queen, being defended by only the Knight, is in difficulties. But we must force Black’s hand, else he escapes by ... xd2+. What we need is a forcing move which reduces Black’s choice of a reply; we look for a capture or a check. Therefore: 1 e7+.
items.label: 176A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 177A. White moves. His Rook menaces Black’s Bishop, which is guarded by his Knight, which in turn is guarded by a Pawn. To remove the guard, it is necessary to “destroy the house that Jack built” by removing the Pawn that guards the Knight that guards the Bishop.
items.label: 177A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 175B. White moves. He has forced a position where the pinned piece (the Queen) is of greater value than the sacrificial Rook. Now 2 h8+ is successful, for it forcibly tears away Black’s King from the defense of his Queen. After 2 ... xh8; 3 xg6 White has an easy win.
items.label: 175B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 176B. Black moves. If 1 ... xe7, the Queen’s guard is removed, allowing 2 xd4. Therefore Black must play 1 ... d8 or 1 ... b8. The problem is still “Delenda est Carthago!” – remove the guard! We accomplish this with another check (priority of check!) by playing 2 xc6+. Now Black’s defense topples. White will play 3 xd4.
items.label: 176B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 178A. Black moves. He sees that the weak link in his opponent’s game is the Bishop. This piece is guarded only by means of other pieces. Black removes the guard by 1 ... xc3, forcing 2 bxc3. White’s defense is about to collapse.

items.caption: 178B. Black moves. He has knocked out one guard. The Pawn push 2 ... g5 disposes of the remaining guard. White has the sad choice of moving the Knight and losing the Bishop, or of saving the Bishop and losing the Knight.
items.label: 178B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD

items.caption: 179A. White moves. He is a piece down, but can regain it with 1 xe4+, xe4; 2 e5+ etc. But he wants something more forceful. White works out a daring idea by removing the guard: 1 xc5!!, xf3.

Knowing what to look for, Black begins with a forcible move, a capture: 1 ... xd4; 2 xd4. Now another forcible move, a threat: 2 ... c5 attacking White’s Queen.

items.caption: 194B. White moves. The menaced Knight must retreat, and he has only one square for the purpose: h2. But by going there (3 h2), he robs the Bishop of its only flight square. items.caption: 195B. White moves. He executes his plan with 2 f5 forcing 2 ... h5. Now 3 g4 wins the Bishop, which is attacked and has no retreat. Trapping a Bishop inside a web of Pawns is a fairly frequently seen stratagem. It has some similarity to the method used in Diagram 191.

203A. Black moves. He sees an opportunity for a skewer attack in the diagonal placement of White’s Bishop on c4 and his Rook at a2. The two pieces are in line, and there ought to be a way ...

items.caption: 203B. White moves. He is trapped in a classic example of the skewer attack. The previous exchange placed two of White’s major pieces in line on the same diagonal. Major pieces always make good targets, as they can rarely afford capture when menaced by minor pieces. White must discreetly withdraw the Queen; after 3 e2, xa2; 4 xa2 etc. he has lost the exchange without any compensation.

items.caption: 204A. Black moves. He can create a skewer attack by forcing the substitution of White’s King for White’s Bishop. In that case, White will be susceptible to a powerful check by Black’s Bishop. Now for the mechanics: we start with a forcing move, therefore 1 ... xf3+. White must recapture: 2 xf3.
items.label: 204A

items.caption: 206A. Black moves. His opponent’s King and Queen are in line on the diagonal. Is a skewer attack possible? Apparently not, as White’s Bishop guards the critical diagonal. But if we can drive the Bishop off, then the skewer will be possible. Therefore: 1 ... f5. The White Bishop cannot be protected, so White plays 2 h4.

But if we can drive the Bishop off, then the skewer will be possible. Therefore: 1 ... f5. The White Bishop cannot be protected, so White plays 2 h4.
items.label: 206A

items.caption: 204B. Black moves. He has brought about a position where two major enemy pieces occupy the same diagonal – an ideal target for the skewer. Black plays 2 ... g4+. After White moves his King away, 3 ... xd1 leaves Black a piece ahead. The Rook was the real target of Black’s combination.
items.label: 204B

items.caption: 205B. White plays. By sheer force, he has produced a position ripe for the skewer. Black’s King and Rook are in line on the diagonal. White strikes at both pieces with 2 f2+. After Black’s King moves, White captures the Rook with a piece ahead. Again the Rook was the target.
items.label: 205B

items.caption: 206B. Black moves. The hindrance to the skewer has been driven off, so that 2 ... h6+ is now possible. This attacks not only the King, but White’s Queen as well. White must play 3 f4, allowing 3 ... exf4+ with complete collapse. (White’s Queen will now be lost just the same. How?)
items.label: 206B

items.caption: 208A. Black moves. He is so far behind in material (Rook for Queen) that only a miracle can save him. The miracle is available, for the White King and Queen are in line, making possible a skewer in veiled form. At the moment 1 ... b1+ is meaningless, as White’s Bishop on b5 stops the skewer. The Bishop must be removed: 1 ... c6+!

items.caption: 209A. White moves. He has two possible captures: 1 xg2 (which wins) or 1 xf7 (which loses). Like Portia’s suitors, he makes the wrong choice: 1 xf7. The move looks attractive, for it threatens mate and leaves Black with (apparently) nothing but a desperate check or two. But Black heads straight for a skewer! – 1 ... h1+; 2 g3, xh3+; 3 f4.
items.label: 209A

items.caption: 207B. White moves. He would like to play 2 b8+ (the skewer!) but is prevented by Black’s Knight. He studies the position some more. His Rooks are doubled on the file, so why fear the Knight capture? White continues the planned attack: 2 b8+!, xb8; 3 xb8+, e7; 4 xh8. The skewer has impaled Black’s Rook after all!
items.label: 207B

items.caption: 209B. Black moves. He has driven White’s King to the f-file, so that both their majesties are in line. With the chief actors in their proper places, we are ready for the skewer: 3 ... f3+. White’s King must step aside, letting the skewer penetrate to his Queen (4 ... xf7).
items.label: 209B

items.caption: 210A. Black moves. He threatens mate at g2, but this is prevented by White’s Queen. But at c2 the Queen is undefended, which gives Black the idea of trying to work out a skewer attack. He needs forcing moves for this, and he has them: plenty of checks.
items.label: 210A

items.caption: 210A. Black moves. He threatens mate at g2, but this is prevented by White’s Queen. But at c2 the Queen is undefended, which gives Black the idea of trying to work out a skewer attack. He needs forcing moves for this, and he has them: plenty of checks.
items.label: 210A

items.caption: 211A. Black moves. As we know, the favorable elements for a skewer attack are in evidence. White’s Queen is unguarded; his King can be forced back to the second rank, where it will be in line with the White Queen. Play proceeds logically:

items.caption: 212A. White moves. We look for forcing moves, noting that Black has only a limited number of King moves in reply. In such situations the defender is generally helpless to change the inexorable course of events, and he is frequently forced into a skewer position. We begin with 1 d7+, h6 (other King moves allow a mate in one); 2 g7+, h5.
items.label: 212A

items.caption: 210B. Black moves. He has brought about the desired position by means of two checks. Now comes the skewer with 3 ... h2+ (or, if you wish, 3 ... g2+ – a matter of taste). After White’s King moves, Black plays 4 ... xc2 and it is all over. This type of skewer attack is quite frequent and deserves careful study. See 211A for a very similar procedure.
items.label: 210B

items.caption: 212B. White moves. He is almost ready now for the skewer, aimed at Black’s Queen. First 3 h7+, forcing 3 ... g4. Now Black’s King and Queen are in line – the maximum objective of a skewer attack. White plays 4 xg6+, and the attack pierces through to win the unfortunate Black Queen, as White ends up with 5 xg1.
items.label: 212B

217A. White moves. Follow ing the basic rule for the handling of Passed Pawns, he plays 1 c7. Passed Pawns must be pushed! White threatens to advance the Pawn now to the queening-square. The only way Black can prevent this is to give up his Queen for the Pawn. Whichever course he takes, White remains a whole Rook ahead, with (of course) an easy win.
items.label: 217A

items.caption: 217B. White moves. His Passed Pawn does not look very formidable.
items.label: 217B

items.caption: 218A. White moves. He has a Passed Pawn on the d-file. His course is clear: advance the Pawn! Hence 1 d6, threatening 2 d7. Black dare not defend with 1 ... d3, for then 2 xd3, xd3; 3 d7 and the Passed Pawn becomes a Queen. Therefore Black blockades the Passed Pawn with 1 ... d7. White promptly attacks the blockader with 2 c6.
