items.caption: 219A. White moves. He has a Passed Pawn on f6, but apparently there is no way to advance it. Black’s Queen blockades its advance; the Black Bishop exerts pressure on the next square of the Pawn’s march; Black’s Rook guards the last rank. But White applies the magic formula: Remove the blockader!
items.label: 219A

items.caption: 220A. White moves. He has many winning lines, but the great Paul Morphy, famous for the elegance of his attacking play, naturally seeks the quickest way. His e-Pawn is already advanced to the seventh rank. What stops its promotion? The Black Queen. Therefore that piece must be removed, and here is how it is done: 1 e6+!, xe6 (forced); 2 dxe6.
items.label: 220A

items.caption: 218B. Black moves. Alas, his blockader (the Knight at d7) must leave his post: 2 ... b8, attacking the Bishop. White replies 3 e8, controlling the next square in the Pawn’s path. Thus all further blockade is impossible. After 4 d7, Black will have to give up his Knight for the Pawn to prevent it from queening. The extra piece will win easily.
items.label: 218B

items.caption: 219B. White moves. The two obstacles to the Passed Pawn’s advance have been thrust aside, and the Pawn (which should have been kept “under lock and key”) advances: 2 f7! Passed Pawns must be pushed! Black is helpless against the specter of the Pawn’s promotion. There followed: 2 ... d8; 3 f8()+, xf8; 4 xf8+ winning the Queen.
items.label: 219B

items.caption: 221A. Black moves. He is confronted with the imminent queening of White’s Passed Pawn. As the queening-square is covered by White’s Bishop, the promotion of the Passed Pawn will cost Black his Rook. He therefore plays 1 ... xa4, intending to answer the obvious 2 bxa4 with ... e8 – after which the worst will have been avoided.
items.label: 221A

items.caption: 221A. Black moves. He is confronted with the imminent queening of White’s Passed Pawn. As the queening-square is covered by White’s Bishop, the promotion of the Passed Pawn will cost Black his Rook. He therefore plays 1 ... xa4, intending to answer the obvious 2 bxa4 with ... e8 – after which the worst will have been avoided.
items.label: 221A

items.caption: 222A. Black moves. He wants to push his Passed Pawn to f2 and f1, acquiring a Queen. But White’s Bishop at c5 prevents the advance of the Passed Pawn. 1 ... f4 looks like a good try, but then 2 f2 stops the Passed Pawn. We must proceed according to the slogan Remove the blockader! The right way is 1 ... c4+. White plays 2 d2 edging nearer to the dangerous Passed Pawn.
items.label: 222A

items.caption: 223A. Black moves. There is no Passed Pawn yet. But by means of a startling sacrifice Black will create a Passed Pawn. Then, according to principle, he will advance the Passed Pawn to the queening-square. He begins with 1 ... f4+, forcing 2 c2. Now he creates the Passed Pawn with 2 ... xg2!
items.label: 223A

items.caption: 221B. White moves. But he does not care to play the obvious recapture! He studies the situation: he has a Passed Pawn, and Passed Pawns must be pushed! What stops the Pawn from queening? The Rook. Therefore the Rook must be removed! White plays 2 d1! (threat: 3 d8+, xd8; 4 exd8()+ and wins). Black tries 2 ... e8 but must lose after 3 d8! pinning.
items.label: 221B

items.caption: 223B. White moves. Having no better reply, he accepts the sacrifice by 3 xg2. In return for the piece, Black has a powerful Passed Pawn. He advances it at once: 3 ... h3. No matter how White plays now, he cannot prevent the Passed Pawn from queening! (Prove this.) Another clever Capablanca ending.
items.label: 223B

items.caption: 223B. White moves. Having no better reply, he accepts the sacrifice by 3 xg2. In return for the piece, Black has a powerful Passed Pawn. He advances it at once: 3 ... h3. No matter how White plays now, he cannot prevent the Passed Pawn from queening! (Prove this.) Another clever Capablanca ending.
items.label: 223B

items.caption: 224A. Black moves. The imminent promotion of his Passed Pawn on the b-file is prevented by White’s Queen, which acts as “goal-keeper.” To break through the defense, it is necessary for Black to control the queening-square. Hence he plays 1 ... e4+, so that if 2 g1, b1(), he is a whole Queen ahead! White tries 2 f3.
items.label: 224A

items.caption: 225A. Black moves. He would like to queen his Passed Pawn without loss of time. But see all the difficulties: White’s Knight controls the queening-square; his King threatens to advance toward the precious Pawn and capture it; finally, Black’s Bishop is attacked. But one startling move changes the picture: 1 ... b2!
items.label: 225A

items.caption: 226A. Black moves. He has a considerable advantage in material, and his Passed Pawn has a clear road ahead of it. But advancing the Passed Pawn is premature, for example 1 ... d2?; 2 g7+, h8 (not 2 ... h6??; 3 g8 mate!); 3 g8+ and Black’s King cannot escape the perpetual check. Relying on the Passed Pawn he plays 1 ... g4+!
items.label: 226A

items.caption: 224B. Black moves. His Queen is attacked. Instead of moving it away, he observes the maxim Passed Pawns must be pushed! He therefore plays 2 ... b1(), for now White’s Queen is also attacked. If 3 fxe4, xd1+. No matter what White does on his third move, he must remain a Queen behind. Note the immediately decisive effect of controlling the queening-square.
items.label: 224B

items.caption: 225B. White moves. His hopes have been dashed. His Knight is an overworked piece: if 2 xb2, c1()+. The Bishop is tabu, but he controls the queening-square; so that if 2 e2 (trying to approach the Passed Pawn), c1(); 3 xc1, xc1 and Black’s material advantage gives him an easy win. A Passed Pawn is no longer a “humble” or “lowly” Pawn.
items.label: 225B

items.caption: 226B. White moves. He has no good continuation. If 2 h2, xg8; 3 xg8, xg8 and White cannot prevent the Passed Pawn from marching on to become a Queen. No better for White is 2 xg4, hxg4+. If White were not in check now, he could play 3 d5 or 3 f5, followed by 4 e3 stopping the Passed Pawn. But priority of check forces White to play a King move, allowing 3 ... d2 etc.
items.label: 226B

items.caption: 227A. Black moves. He has a deep plan for making use of his Passed Pawn on e3. He begins with 1 ... c7, intensifying the pin on the Knight. 2 f6+ is refuted by 2 ... xf6; 3 xf6, e2 (threatens 4 ... d1+, as in 221B); 4 c1, cd7 and wins. White therefore tries 2 hd1. Momentarily his Knight is adequately guarded.
items.label: 227A

items.caption: 227B. Black moves. He has two ways of utilizing his Passed Pawn. One is: 2 ... e2, making White’s attacked Rook an overworked piece. If it moves on the file, then the Pawn advances and becomes a Queen; if the Rook moves on the rank, then White’s Knight is lost. The second method is: 2 ... cxd7; 3 xd7, xd7; 4 xd7, e2! and queens.
items.label: 227B

items.caption: 228A. White moves. In 226 and 227 we have seen the value of simplifying in order to exploit the strength of a Passed Pawn. Here the combination begins with 1 xf6! forcing 1 ... gxf6.
items.label: 228A

items.caption: 229. White moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing by Black’s King. How does he drive off the blockader and win the game?
229. White moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing by Black’s King. How does he drive off the blockader and win the game?
230. Black moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing to the queening-square by White’s Bishop. How does Black get rid of the Bishop?

231. White moves. He is ahead in material and has several ways of winning. The quickest method is to simplify by sacrificing, so that his Passed Pawn can march on irresistibly. How does White accomplish this?

233A. Black is checkmated. Offhand it might seem that he had been a bit careless and overlooked the mate pictured in the diagram. That this is not the case, can be seen from the next diagram, which shows how this position came about. Later on, we shall see that the weakness of the first rank often makes remarkable combinations possible. Sometimes the result is outright mate, as here; other times, exploitation is indirect.
items.label: 233A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 233A. Black is checkmated. Offhand it might seem that he had been a bit careless and overlooked the mate pictured in the diagram. That this is not the case, can be seen from the next diagram, which shows how this position came about. Later on, we shall see that the weakness of the first rank often makes remarkable combinations possible. Sometimes the result is outright mate, as here; other times, exploitation is indirect.
items.label: 233A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 233B. White moves. Spotting the weakness of Black’s first rank, he plays 1 xa8! The sacrifice is decisive, because it removes one of the defenders of Black’s first rank. After 1 ... xa8 Black has only one Rook guarding his d8, while White has two Rooks trained on it. There follows: 2 d8+, xd8; 3 xd8 mate, as in 233A. In such situations, the creation of a “loophole” by (say) ... h6 is advisable.
items.label: 233B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 234A. Black moves. His Queen and a Rook are trained on White’s first rank, which is guarded by a Rook and Bishop. But the Bishop, being pinned, is paralyzed. Therefore the first rank is vulnerable to attack. Black can invade by sacrificing his Queen: 1 ... e1+! forcing 2 xe1.
items.label: 234A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 235A. White moves. It seems difficult if not impossible to penetrate Black’s first rank. Yet it can be done; and if we look for all possible checks and captures, we find the violent move 1 xd7+! Black plays 1 ... xd7 (1 ... b8 avoids mate but leads to frightful loss of material).
items.label: 235A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 236A. White moves. He attacks the h-Pawn twice, and it is defended only once. Not realizing that his Queen is tied to the defense of the first rank, he plays 1 xh5? With this capture, White’s first rank becomes vulnerable. To prove this, Black sacrifices his Queen with 1 ... xh5! As he cannot remain a Rook down, White retakes: 2 xh5.
items.label: 236A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 235B. White moves. He continues with occupation of the vulnerable rank: 2 e8+. Black must interpose by 2 ... d8. Now either White Rook captures the Rook, giving checkmate. The brilliant sacrifice 1 xd7+! was perpetrated in actual play by Paul Keres on World Champion Alekhine.
items.label: 235B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 235B. White moves. He continues with occupation of the vulnerable rank: 2 e8+. Black must interpose by 2 ... d8. Now either White Rook captures the Rook, giving checkmate. The brilliant sacrifice 1 xd7+! was perpetrated in actual play by Paul Keres on World Champion Alekhine.
items.label: 235B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 236B. Black moves. He swoops down the whole length of the open file: 2 ... c1+. White interposes with 3 f1; perhaps he overlooks the long-range effect of Black’s Bishop at a6! Black now follows through with 3 ... xf1 mate. (Had White played 3 d1, he would have delayed the mate for one move.) The Queen sacrifice was startling but logical.
items.label: 236B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 237A. Black moves. He wants to invade White’s first rank via the e-file. The play in 235A tells us what to look for. Searching for forcing moves such as checks or captures, Black decides in favor of 1 ... axd2 White recaptures by 2 xd2. (If 2 xd2, xd2; 3 xd2, e1 mate!)
items.label: 237A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 238A. White moves. His Queen and Rook are doubled on the c-file – one of the surest methods of dominating an open line. Such control enables one to use the file as a “jumping-off place” for forcible entry into the hostile position. The opponent’s first rank is a favorite target for this type of attack. White plays 1 g3 with a double threat.
items.label: 238A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 239A. Black moves. It is not clear how he can work up an attack against White’s first rank. But the process of looking for checks and captures again gives us a priceless hint. We begin with 1 ... f3+, which forces White’s King to g1 in order to keep the Rook guarded. Now White’s first rank is vulnerable. The search for checks and captures yields a delightful sequel: 2 ... xf1+!
items.label: 239A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 237B. Black moves. By sacrificing the exchange, he has rendered White’s first rank vulnerable to invasion. Two of the defenders of White’s e1 are gone, so that Black can play 2 ... e1+!; 3 xe1 (or 3 f2, e3 mate), xe1 mate. Black’s first move was an example of removing the guard.
items.label: 237B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 238B. Black moves. His Knight is attacked; hence 1 ... g6, parrying the threat. But White had another threat, made possible by the retreat of the Bishop. This menace, far from obvious, now becomes reality: 2 c8+, xc8; 3 xc8 mate! Black could have avoided this mate, but only at the cost of leaving his attacked Knight in the lurch.
items.label: 238B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 239B. White moves. He has only one reply, 3 xf1, which is resoundingly answered by 3 ... d1 mate. Black’s Pawn at f3 acts as a powerful wedge (actually doing the work of a Bishop or Queen) in blocking the escape of the White King. All of Black’s moves were violent: the more stringently the defense is limited, the easier it is to foresee the consequences.
items.label: 239B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 240A. White moves. He begins with 1 c4+ (1 b3+ has the same effect), which is as strong as it is obvious. Strong because it drives Black’s King into the corner, which makes his first rank vulnerable; obvious because all checks and captures are obvious – they must be the first moves one looks at. Black is forced (why?) to play 1 ... h8. Now comes the brilliant 2 f7!
items.label: 240A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 241A. White moves. He plans to drive Black’s King into the corner. As in 240A, Black’s King will have no mobility – no space to move freely if checked. Knowing what to look for, White plays the brilliant 1 xg7+! Black replies 1 ... xg7 (1 ... h8 allows mate in two – how?). The play continues 2 f7+, h8.
items.label: 241A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 242A. White moves. He plays the “brilliant” move 1 xf6?, reckoning on 1 ... gxf6; 2 xf6+ and mate next move. But, by removing his Rook from the first rank, White has weakened that line. Black reasons that if the other Rook disappears, the vulnerable first rank will be open to mating threats. This leads to the forcing 1 ... xa1!
items.label: 242A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 240B. Black moves. There is no adequate defense to the threat of 3 xg7 mate. If Black plays 3 ... xf7; 4 xe8+ forcing mate next move on the vital rank. 3 ... g8 guards the mate, but 4 xe8 has catastrophic consequences for Black. The chief cause of Black’s downfall is the uselessness of his Queen. Successful attack or efficient defense is difficult without the Queen.
items.label: 240B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 241B. White moves. His brilliant next move should be seen in a flash – look for checks and captures! Black’s first rank, guarded only by a Rook, is attacked by White’s Queen and Rook. How can this concentrated menace be utilized? Answer: 3 f8+! xf8; 4 xf8 mate. Four consecutive checks, two of them captures, led to Black’s downfall.
items.label: 241B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 243A. White moves. He has two attacking “batteries”, the Queen, Bishop and f-Pawn operate against g7; the Rooks control the only open line. To obtain the cooperation of all these forces, he uses a discovered attack: 1 xd7!, xd7; 2 f6! (This Pawn has been unpinned by the sacrifice of the exchange.)
items.label: 243A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 243A. White moves. He has two attacking “batteries”, the Queen, Bishop and f-Pawn operate against g7; the Rooks control the only open line. To obtain the cooperation of all these forces, he uses a discovered attack: 1 xd7!, xd7; 2 f6! (This Pawn has been unpinned by the sacrifice of the exchange.)
items.label: 243A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 244A. Black moves. He must not snatch at the Queen: 1 ... xb7??; 2 xe8+, xe8; 3 xe8 mate – vulnerable first rank! Instead, Black plays the startling but logical 1 ... xe2! making use of the same weapon to checkmate White! After 2 xe2 White’s first rank is vulnerable. Black proves this immediately as his Rook whizzes down the open file: 2 ... c1+.
items.label: 244A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 245A. White moves. His first observation is that Black’s Rooks are disconnected – always a likely indication of a weak first rank. But White’s goal is not mate; he sees that he can only force the win of a piece. After 1 xb4, xb4; 2 d2 there is a double attack menacing the Rook at b5 and also threatening 3 d8+, xd8; 4 xd8 mate.
items.label: 245A
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 243B. Black moves. He is confronted with two threats: 3 xd7 or 3 fxg7+, which wins at least a Rook. To parry both threats, he is forced to play 2 ... fd8. But White wins anyway: 3 xd7! After 3 ... xd7 Black’s first rank is denuded of defenders. He is helpless against the deadly Rook move: 4 e8 mate.
items.label: 243B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 244B. White moves. He cannot stave off mate, but he has a venomous last trap. If he tries 3 e1, then 3 ... xe1+; 4 xe1, xe1 mate. Instead, White plays 3 e1, inviting the blunder 3 ... xe2?? when 4 b8+ (or 4 a8+) forces checkmate on Black! But Black is wary: he plays 3 ... xe1+! 4 xe1, xe1 mate. These witty possibilities deserve careful study.
items.label: 244B
items.chapter_title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 246. White moves. What is the quickest way to remove the guardian of Black’s first rank, making the Black King vulnerable to mate next move?
items.chapter_title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 246. White moves. What is the quickest way to remove the guardian of Black’s first rank, making the Black King vulnerable to mate next move?
items.chapter_title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 247. White moves. He cannot force mate, but he can make use of the vulnerable first rank idea to queen his Passed Pawn. How? (Hint: see 221B.)
items.chapter_title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 248. White moves. His situation is apparently critical, for if he plays 1 d6 (forced?) there follows 1 ... xe1+; 2 f2, e4+. Yet White can win by exploiting Black’s vulnerable first rank. How?
items.chapter_title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK

items.caption: 250A. Black moves. His powerful pressure against the h-Pawn is neutralized by White’s Queen. Black breaks the line of communication by 1 ... d3!!
items.label: 250A

items.caption: 250A. Black moves. His powerful pressure against the h-Pawn is neutralized by White’s Queen. Black breaks the line of communication by 1 ... d3!!
items.label: 250A

items.caption: 250B. White moves. If he plays 2 xd3, Black continues 2 ... xh3+; 3 g1, g2 mate. Or if 2 xd3, xd3; 3 xd3, d6+ (double attack!) and wins.
items.label: 250B

items.caption: 251A. Black moves. His Bishop attacks White’s Knight, which is protected by his Rook. The Rook cannot be driven off, nor threatened with capture or exchange. Yet its protective power can be nullified by 1 ... d2+, forcing 2 c1.
items.label: 251A

items.caption: 251B. Black moves. He still attacks the Knight, but it is no longer guarded by the Rook. The line of communication has been snapped by the forced retreat of White’s King. Consequently Black wins easily by simply removing the Knight: 2 ... xe1.
items.label: 251B

items.caption: 252A. Black moves. He plays to win a Pawn, without realizing that he will be breaking the line of communication that guards a vital piece. He captures by 1 ... gxf4 and after 2 gxf4, he snatches the seemingly undefended Pawn by 2 ... xf4?
items.label: 252A

items.caption: 252B. White moves. His Queen attacks Black’s Queen, which is protected by a Rook. He severs the line of communication with 3 g3+. If now 3 ... f7, Black’s Queen has lost the protection of the Rook, so that 4 xf4+ wins at once.
items.label: 252B

items.caption: 253A. White moves. He pins and doubly attacks Black’s Bishop at e7, which is doubly defended. To drive away Black’s Queen from the defense, White plays 1 f4. Now Black cannot play 1 ... xf4?? (removal of the guard) because of 2 xe7 mate. Or, if 1 ... f6, the skewer 2 g5 makes the pin decisive. Black therefore tries 1 ... c5.
items.label: 253A

items.caption: 253B. White moves. He plays 2 d6, striking for the third time at the pinned Bishop, which is overwhelmed, as it is attacked three times and defended only once. The d-Pawn has added its weight to the attack; but more important is the fact that it has wedged itself between Bishop and Queen, cutting their line of communication. Black is lost; if 2 ... cxd6; 3 xe7 mate.
items.label: 253B

items.caption: 254B. Black moves. With the venomous Pawn push 2 ... b5, he breaks the line of communication, attacking the Queen and winning the Bishop. Creating a line of communication in order to break it is a novel device! There is an analogy in the story of the preacher who was exhorting his congregation to repent, and save themselves from the lot of sinners in the Hereafter – where “There will be weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth.” “Suppose I have no teeth?” an old lady asked. “Teeth will be provided,” was the preacher’s quick reply.
items.label: 254B

items.caption: 255A. Black moves. He invades enemy territory by 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. It is relatively best for White to make a temporary escape with 2 h3, with a prosaic loss in prospect. But he instinctively guards the weak spot with 2 f1?
items.label: 255A

items.caption: 255A. Black moves. He invades enemy territory by 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. It is relatively best for White to make a temporary escape with 2 h3, with a prosaic loss in prospect. But he instinctively guards the weak spot with 2 f1?
items.label: 255A

items.caption: 256A. White moves. He has given up a piece for a strong attack, which is all the more virulent because Black’s Queen is cut off from the defense. For his concluding combination, he has prepared a charming sacrifice. He plays 1 g7+ forcing 1 ... f7. And now the sur prise: 2 e6+!!
items.label: 256A

items.caption: 257A. White moves. How can his Queen participate in the attack with no loss of time? To avoid giving Black a breathing spell, White plays 1 b5! Black must do something about his Queen – at once! Therefore he has no time to attend to his King’s welfare. Black replies 1 ... xb5 (other Queen moves allow the same continuation).
items.label: 257A

items.caption: 255B. Black moves. He has a surprise move: 2 ... xf3! White captures by 3 gxf3, whereupon Black gracefully winds up the White King’s career with 3 ... g6 mate – an “epaulet” mate! The White Rooks which hover so anxiously around their King actually bring about his downfall!
items.label: 255B

items.caption: 256B. Black moves. Rocked on his heels by the unexpected Queen sacrifice, he has no choice but to accept: 2 ... xe6. The capture is answered by 3 dxe6 mate! Despite the army of White pieces trained on Black’s King, it remained for the not-so-humble Pawn to deal the death -blow!
items.label: 256B

items.caption: 257B. White moves. His clever Bishop sacrifice cleared the way for action by the Queen – but not at once (2 h5??, f1 mate!). Again time is of the essence – another violent move is needed: 2 xh7+!, forcing 2 ... xh7. Now White mates by 3 h5+, h6; 4 xh6 mate. “Surprise is nothing more than logic that packs a wallop.”
items.label: 257B

items.caption: 258A. White moves. Threatened with mate on the move, he hits on the superb surprise move 1 b6+!! Pundits would analyze this fearless plunge into a nest of hostile Pawns as a Knight fork, based on a pin (Black’s c-Pawn is paralyzed), plus a sacrifice as a clearance for the White Queen. But for our purposes the Knight move is a magnificent stroke, too delightful to desecrate by dissection!
items.label: 258A

items.caption: 259A. Black moves. He sees the three-move threat of mate with 1 h7+, f8; 2 e6+, fxe6; 3 xg7 mate. What more natural than 1 ... xd4 parrying the threat and winning a piece? But Black gets a rude awakening, as White replies with the electrifying 2 h8+.
items.label: 259A

items.caption: 258B. Black moves. He captures: 1 ... axb6. Utilizing the open a- file, White replies 2 a8 mate. (Black could have avoided the mate by moving his King in reply to 1 b6+!! – but this would have meant losing the Queen.)
items.label: 258B

items.caption: 259B. Black moves. He has no choice: he must play 2 ... xh8, allowing 3 xh8 mate. The Queen sacrifice seems a lot less startling to one who is familiar with mating patterns (see the section on that subject). An early combination by Dr. Euwe, who later became World Champion.
items.label: 259B

items.caption: 259B. Black moves. He has no choice: he must play 2 ... xh8, allowing 3 xh8 mate. The Queen sacrifice seems a lot less startling to one who is familiar with mating patterns (see the section on that subject). An early combination by Dr. Euwe, who later became World Champion.
items.label: 259B

items.caption: 261A. White moves. He is the exchange ahead – enough to win, but there is no obvious immediate decision. However, White has a beautiful surprise move which gives Black his quietus: 1 d5!!, offering his Rook in four different ways! Despite these alternative ways of capturing, the White Rook is anything but vulnerable.
items.label: 261A

items.caption: 261A. White moves. He is the exchange ahead – enough to win, but there is no obvious immediate decision. However, White has a beautiful surprise move which gives Black his quietus: 1 d5!!, offering his Rook in four different ways! Despite these alternative ways of capturing, the White Rook is anything but vulnerable.
items.label: 261A

items.caption: 262A. Black moves. Since White’s King cannot move, mate can be administered by any Black checking piece safe from capture. This is the logical explanation of the extraordinary play that follows: 1 ... xb2!! threatening 2 ... xh2 mate. If now 2 h3, h2 or if 2 h1, e1, forcing mate in either case. White prefers to be “shown.” He plays 2 xb2, which is answered by the stunning 2 ... e5!!
items.label: 262A

items.caption: 261B. Black moves. Which way does he want to be mated? If 1 xd5; 2 f6 mate (overworked Queen). If 1 ... xd5; 2 f8 mate (vulnerable first rank). Finally, if 1 ... exd5 or 1 ... xd5; 2 xd8 mate (breaking communications)! Nor can Black really refuse the Rook, as 2 xd8 mate and 2 xd4 are threatened.
items.label: 261B

items.caption: 261B. Black moves. Which way does he want to be mated? If 1 xd5; 2 f6 mate (overworked Queen). If 1 ... xd5; 2 f8 mate (vulnerable first rank). Finally, if 1 ... exd5 or 1 ... xd5; 2 xd8 mate (breaking communications)! Nor can Black really refuse the Rook, as 2 xd8 mate and 2 xd4 are threatened.
items.label: 261B

items.caption: 262B. White moves. Life is still very difficult for him, the threat being 3 ... g6 mate! He has no alternative but to play 3 fxe5. But now the real blow descends, for Black’s earlier sacrifices, brilliant though they were, served only as preliminaries. Black plays 3 ... g5 mate! It was the fatal position of the White King that made the surprise moves logical.
items.label: 262B

items.caption: 264. Black moves. He sees that 1 ... h3+ wins against all four possible replies: if 2 gxh3, xf2+; 3 h1, xh2 mate. If 2 xh3, xe4, and White’s overworked Rook cannot recapture; for if 3 xe4, d1+ leads to mate on the vulnerable first rank. If 2 f1, xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. Finally, if 2 h1, xf2+ wins the Queen by a Knight fork.

264. Black moves. He sees that 1 ... h3+ wins against all four possible replies: if 2 gxh3, xf2+; 3 h1, xh2 mate. If 2 xh3, xe4, and White’s overworked Rook cannot recapture; for if 3 xe4, d1+ leads to mate on the vulnerable first rank. If 2 f1, xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. Finally, if 2 h1, xf2+ wins the Queen by a Knight fork.

265A. Black moves. He sees an attractive Knight fork which threatens King and Queen: 1 ... e4+. But White has a Pawn guarding the crucial square! The unthinking player would discard the idea at this point; but one familiar with combination patterns looks further ahead. He makes the impossible moves become possible! Black plays 1 ... e4+! forcing 2 fxe4.
items.label: 265A

items.caption: 266A. White moves. Will it be giving away the plot to say that White wins material by a combination involving a Knight fork followed by a pin? The first link in the chain is an attack on Black’s Queen: 1 g5. (His object, improbable as it may seem, is to play 2 e6, forking the Black Rooks.) Black replies 1 ... e8, hoping to guard the vital square.
items.label: 266A

items.caption: 267A. White moves. He notes that the mobility of Black’s Queen is severely constricted. How can White exploit this state of affairs? He looks for a violent move. 1 b4, attacking the Queen and unpinning the Knight, answers the purpose. After the forced reply 1 ... b6, White follows up with 2 xd5, this time forcing 2 ... c6.
items.label: 267A

items.caption: 265B. Black moves. His opponent’s King and Queen are in line, making possible a pin on the King Bishop file. 2 ... f8 wins White’s Queen. Black has combined two familiar patterns, the Knight fork and the pin, to form his winning combination. Heaven-sent inspiration? No! Black succeeded because he knew what to look for!
items.label: 265B

items.caption: 266B. White moves. His intended invasion is prevented, but only ostensibly so. As a combination player (one who is familiar with the basic winning patterns), White is not discouraged: he merely looks one move ahead and plays 2 e6! menacing both Rooks. After 2 ... xe6 he plays 3 xf4! exploiting the pin on Black’s e-Pawn. White has won the exchange.
items.label: 266B

items.caption: 267B. White moves. Should he retreat his attacked Knight? No, because he has a stronger move. Note that Black’s King and Queen are in line. This makes a pin possible: 3 b5. The pin works even though the Bishop is unguarded: 3 ... xb5 is answered by the picturesque family check 4 xc7+ winning the Queen with an easy win.
items.label: 267B

items.caption: 268A. White moves. He has given up two Pawns to reach this promising combinative position. After 1 xe6, fxe6 he can regain one of the lost Pawns by 2 f4, attacking the Queen and King’s Pawn. But this pedestrian continuation is not good enough. After studying every check and capture, he plays 2 xe6+!
items.label: 268A

items.caption: 269A. Black moves. White’s centrally posted Bishop and Knight are insecure, as they are not guarded by Pawns. This calls for the powerful but fairly obvious 1 ... e8, striking at the Bishop and the pinned Knight behind it. 2 f4 is now forced, and play continues 2 ... xe4, this time forcing 3 xe4.
items.label: 269A

items.caption: 270A. White moves. In the most innocent-looking positions, there often lurk deadly but delightful combinations. Who would suspect that White can impale his opponent’s King and Queen by a pin, or run them through with a skewer? To combine these motifs – that is the art of chess. 1 d8+ forces 1 ... f7; now 2 e6+! is decisive.
items.label: 270A

items.caption: 268B. Black moves. His King and Queen are attacked by the impudent, unprotected Rook, which must be captured. In the words of the Queen of Hearts, “Off with his head!” Black plays 2 ... xe6. But now White trumps this trick with 3 xg7+, an attractive Knight fork which wins the Queen.
items.label: 268B

items.caption: 269B. Black moves. White’s pinned Knight has disappeared, but his pinned Bishop is now the target. If 3 ... f6 White escapes by counterattack (4 a4). Study every check and capture! This yields the brilliant solution 3 ... c3+! forking King and Queen. 4 dxc3 is impossible; 4 xc3 loses White’s Queen.
items.label: 269B

items.caption: 270B. Black moves. He must capture the fatal Pawn, and either method of capture allows a pretty conclusion. Thus if 2 ... xe6; 3 e8+ wins Black’s Queen by the skewer. Or if 2 ... xe6 the newly unpinned Bishop asserts his freedom with the malevolent 3 c4, pinning (and winning) Black’s Queen. A deceptively simple position!
items.label: 270B

items.caption: 271A. Black moves. He wins a piece by combining three different ideas: Queen sacrifice, Knight fork and vulnerable first rank. This is all less formidable than it sounds. To begin with, he is dissatisfied with 1 ... f2+; 2 xf2, xf2 which merely wins the exchange. If only 2 ... e1+ were feasible! But White can interpose at f1. The solution: 1 ... xd3!!; 2 cxd3.
items.label: 271A

items.caption: 272A. White moves. Broken down into cold technical terms, his delightful combination makes use of a Queen sacrifice to seize the vulnerable last rank. There he pins a defended piece. Another pin, based on a sacrifice, removes the guard. Awe-inspiring as this may sound, the themes are old friends by now: :
items.label: 272A

items.caption: 273A. White moves. Zukertort, who had the White pieces here, was a “sugar-cake” in name only! He begins with the amazing Queen sacrifice 1 b5! The reply 1 ... xb5 is unavoidable, for if 1 ... d7?; 2 c8()+ or 2 xc6+ leaves White a Queen ahead. The combination unfolds with 2 c8()+, f7 (if 2 ... d8? the Knight fork c7+ wins the Queen).
items.label: 273A

items.caption: 272B. White moves. He must remove the guard of the pinned Bishop before Black can consolidate his defense. Therefore 3 xd5 pinning the Queen. Black is lost. He must play 3 ... xd5, else he loses the Queen. But now that the guard is removed, White plays 4 xe8 mate. Again we must admire the slick interplay of several combinative motifs.
items.label: 272B

items.caption: 272B. White moves. He must remove the guard of the pinned Bishop before Black can consolidate his defense. Therefore 3 xd5 pinning the Queen. Black is lost. He must play 3 ... xd5, else he loses the Queen. But now that the guard is removed, White plays 4 xe8 mate. Again we must admire the slick interplay of several combinative motifs.
items.label: 272B

items.caption: 273B. White moves. His next two moves should be seen in a flash by conscientious students of combination patterns. What can White obtain in return for parting with the precious Passed Pawn? The answer: 3 xe6+! xe6 and now the Knight fork 4 c7+ wins Black’s Queen. The upshot of the ingenious combination is that White has won a piece by forcing moves.
items.label: 273B

items.caption: 274A. White moves. His material advantage is enough to win, but he wants victory by the quickest route. Therefore he seeks forcing moves. The indicated target is Black’s f-Pawn, which is on an open file. So White begins with 1 e6. Black defends with 1 ... b7 and White adds more weight to the pin with 2 g6, forcing 2 ... f6.
items.label: 274A

items.caption: 275A. Black moves. His combination hinges on the fact that the two Queens are en prise to each other. He begins with a brutal move (and in chess one must be brutal):
items.label: 275A

items.caption: 276A. White moves. The beautifully intermeshed combination which follows is based on the fact that Black’s Bishop has to guard a Knight and the Queen (overworked piece!), and on the lack of communication between Black’s Rooks. Throughout, we seek checks and captures:
items.label: 276A

items.caption: 274B. White moves. Again on the lookout for violent moves, he breaks through with a sacrifice: 3 xf6+!, xf6 (if 3 ... g8; 4 f7 is decisive). After 4 xf6+ Black must play 4 ... e8 to guard his Rook at d8 from the double attack of White’s Queen. Now White winds up with a skewer: 5 h8+, e7; 6 g7+ (or 6 h7+) winning the Rook at b7.
items.label: 274B

items.caption: 275B. Black moves. Now for the pretty point of the combination: 3 ... f3+!, forking King and Queen. If White moves his King, then 4 ... xd2. If instead 4 xf3 (overworked Rook!), then 4 ... xd2+. In either event, White’s Queen is lost, and with it the game.
items.label: 275B

items.caption: 277A. Black moves. His enormous advantage in position (based on the indirect pin by the Bishop) more than outweighs his material disadvantage. But to translate this into quick victory, he needs forcing moves. He begins with 1 ... xh2! If the Queen is captured (vulnerable first rank), 2 ... f1 mate.
items.label: 277A

items.caption: 277A. Black moves. His enormous advantage in position (based on the indirect pin by the Bishop) more than outweighs his material disadvantage. But to translate this into quick victory, he needs forcing moves. He begins with 1 ... xh2! If the Queen is captured (vulnerable first rank), 2 ... f1 mate.
items.label: 277A

items.caption: 277B. White moves. He plays 2 e1 (if 2 g1, Black has two ways of mating in two moves – how?). Black insists on sacrificing his Queen by 2 ... xe2+! Then if 3 xe2, f2 with double check and mate. Equally pretty is 3 xe2, f1 mate. Being pinned, White’s Rook must stay at e2.
items.label: 277B

items.caption: 278A. White moves. The Black Bishop is pinned! Hence the artistic move 1 f6! Black must not play 1 ... xf6 because of 2 e8 mate. So he tries 1 ... xc3, giving the Bishop more protection.
items.label: 278A

items.caption: 279. White moves. He has several ways of winning, but the quickest is based on a pin, followed by a Knight fork. How would you demonstrate this?
279. White moves. He has several ways of winning, but the quickest is based on a pin, followed by a Knight fork. How would you demonstrate this?
280. White moves. His modus operandi is a discovered attack followed by a Knight fork. What two moves does he play to bring this about?
281. White moves. He can win material by means of a double attack, followed by a pin. How?

283A. White moves. He wants to break through the barrier of Pawns. The indicated target is the g-Pawn. It is guarded by the King, but 1 f6 menaces 2 xg7 mate. Black’s g-Pawn is pinned; hence his only defense is 1 ... g6. But this resource – the only one Black has, to be sure – will prove a flimsy one.

284.White moves. Queen, supported by Bishop, mates at h7.
285. Queen, supported by Pawn wedge at g6, mates at h7.
286.White moves. Queen, supported by Rook, mates on the open file.
287.White moves. Queen, supported by Knight, mates at h7.
288.White moves. Queen, supported by Knight, mates at g7.

291.White moves. Queen, supported by Bishop on the long diagonal, mates at g7 or h8.
292. Rook (or Queen) supported by Bishop on the long diagonal, mates at h8.
293. Rook, supported by Knight at f6, mates at h7 or g8.
294. White moves. Doubled Rooks force mate on the seventh rank.

295. Black moves. Classic position for smothered mate by Queen and Knight. (From a book by Lucena published in 1496!) The winning process after 1 ... h8 is 2 f7+, g8; 3 h6+, h8; 4 g8+!!, xg8; 5 f7 mate!

296A. White moves. All his pieces are trained on Black’s King-side. We see a mating pattern in the attack of Queen and Bishop against h7 (see Diagram 284). For the time being, this target is guarded by Black’s Knight. Therefore the Knight must be removed:
items.label: 296A

items.caption: 297A. White moves. He has an overwhelming attack, based partly on the fact that Black has moved the Pawns in front of his King. This weakness, plus the concentration of White’s forces, promises forceful sacrificial brilliancies to come. White’s Queen is attacked. Instead of retreating the Queen, he relies on the mating pattern of Diagram 292. There follows 1 xf6! Realizing that 1 ... xf6; 2 xh6 is quite hopeless, Black tries 1 ... gxh4.
items.label: 297A

items.caption: 298A. Black moves. His doubled Rooks are very powerful on the seventh rank. Were it not for the protective influence of the White Rook at g4, Black might be able to apply the mating pattern of Diagram 294. This automatically suggests a brilliant sacrifice: 1 ... xg4!; 2 fxg4.
items.label: 298A

items.caption: 297B. White moves. He must now prove the soundness of his Queen sacrifice. How? His Rook has a vital open file and is supported powerfully by the Bishop on f6. White plays 2 xg7+, which is answered by 2 ... f8 (if 2 ... h8; 3 g5 or 3 g4 or 3 g3 mate – the other Bishop also plays a role!). Now we are ready for the pattern of Diagram 292: 3 h7! No squirming can stop h8 mate.
items.label: 297B

items.caption: 297B. White moves. He must now prove the soundness of his Queen sacrifice. How? His Rook has a vital open file and is supported powerfully by the Bishop on f6. White plays 2 xg7+, which is answered by 2 ... f8 (if 2 ... h8; 3 g5 or 3 g4 or 3 g3 mate – the other Bishop also plays a role!). Now we are ready for the pattern of Diagram 292: 3 h7! No squirming can stop h8 mate.
items.label: 297B

items.caption: 299A. White moves. “White’s Knight is strongly posted at f5.” This comment, so often seen in annotations, introduces us to the pattern of Diagram 288. At this advanced post, the Knight offers ideal support for a checkmate with the Queen at g7. How is White’s Queen to get access to the vital square without loss of time? White plays 1 h6! discounting the fact that he leaves his Rook unguarded.
items.label: 299A

items.caption: 299A. White moves. “White’s Knight is strongly posted at f5.” This comment, so often seen in annotations, introduces us to the pattern of Diagram 288. At this advanced post, the Knight offers ideal support for a checkmate with the Queen at g7. How is White’s Queen to get access to the vital square without loss of time? White plays 1 h6! discounting the fact that he leaves his Rook unguarded.
items.label: 299A

items.caption: 300A. White moves. The situation of his attacking forces (Knight on f6 and heavy pieces on the h- and g-files) reminds us irresistibly of the pattern shown on Diagram 293. The theoretically possible mates on h7 or g8 are both prevented by Black’s Rook at g7. The word both suggests that the Rook is overworked. And so it is: 1 xh7+!, xh7.
items.label: 300A

items.caption: 301A. White moves. He has sacrificed a piece, and can regain it if he wishes by 1 hxg6. But he seeks a more forceful line. The position calls to mind the pattern of Diagram 289 Accordingly White plays 1 h6+! renouncing the regain of the piece. The Pawn wedge establishes a powerful bind on the adverse King’s position.
items.label: 301A

items.caption: 299B. Black moves. As he cannot guard his g7, he snaps up the unprotected Rook. But after 1 ... xe1+; 2 f1, we perceive that the fate of the Rook was of no importance. What matters is that White, following the pattern for such positions, threatens 3 g7 mate. To prevent this mate, Black would have to give up his Queen with 2 ... e3+ – a fatal loss of material.
items.label: 299B

items.caption: 301B. Black moves. He gets out of check by 1 ... g8. Now comes 2 f6 and Black is helpless against 3 g7 mate. (The same position results from 1 ... h8; 2 f6+ etc.) In all these examples, the Queen is able to force mate at close range, supported by piece or Pawn. The hostile King cannot touch a piece that is protected.
items.label: 301B

items.caption: 301B. Black moves. He gets out of check by 1 ... g8. Now comes 2 f6 and Black is helpless against 3 g7 mate. (The same position results from 1 ... h8; 2 f6+ etc.) In all these examples, the Queen is able to force mate at close range, supported by piece or Pawn. The hostile King cannot touch a piece that is protected.
items.label: 301B

items.caption: 302A. Black moves. The sweeping diagonal of his Bishop on b7 suggests the pattern of Diagram 292 – all the more so as Black has an open h-file. 1 ... h6 is too slow because of 2 f3, defending h2 and also closing the long diagonal. A violent move is needed: 1 ... xh2!
items.label: 302A

items.caption: 303A. White moves. He plays 1 h5, threatening 2 xh7 mate as in Diagram 287. Remember that the King is absolutely helpless to touch a piece which is protected. Black must play 1 ... h6 to prevent the mate. After 2 xg6 White again threatens mate at h7. White’s Queen is immune from capture, as. Black’s f-Pawn is pinned. Hence 2 ... hxg5 must be played.
items.label: 303A

items.caption: 304A. White moves. His Pawn at g6 reminds us of the mating pattern of Diagram 285. This calls for bringing the Queen to h7; but White’s Rooks are in the way, and he is also threatened with mate. He looks for violent moves:
items.label: 304A

items.caption: 302B. White moves. He is threatened with 2 ... h1 mate, as per pattern. White no longer has the defense 2 f3, for this would allow 2 ... xe2. White plays 2 xh2 and after 2 ... h6+ (2 ... h8+ also works); 3 g1 there follows 3 ... h1 mate. Applying the proper pattern made the Rook sacrifice a routine affair.
items.label: 302B

items.caption: 303B. White moves. His attempt to apply the pattern of Diagram 287 has been foiled. But there are other patterns! He plays 3 xg5, and the momentary threat against the Black Queen gains time for the attack. After 3 ... e8 White plays 4 f6! – with a beautiful double pin. The wedge with the Bishop forces mate (see the pattern of Diagram 290). Black’s pieces are paralyzed by pins.
items.label: 303B

items.caption: 304B. Black moves. These Rook sacrifices are becoming monotonous! Black must again capture, but after 4 ... xh8, the pattern of the desired mate has emerged in clear-cut form: 5 h1+ g8; 6 h7 mate. To complete his design for checkmate, White did not shrink from sacrificing two Rooks. His knowledge of the pattern he needed guided him to a victorious conclusion.
items.label: 304B

items.caption: 305A. White moves. Note how menacingly his Bishops are directed at Black’s King-side. Black’s Achilles heel is his g7, as White demonstrates with 1 g4. (1 d4 looks more natural, but allows Black to defend with ... g5). Black is now embarrassed for a defense to the threatened mate, as he cannot play 1 ... f6 (the Pawn is pinned!) nor can he play 1 ... f6.
items.label: 305A

items.caption: 306A. White moves. He has three pieces trained on Black’s King-side. If he retreats his attacked Bishop, Black will have time to consolidate the defense. Aiming for the pattern of Diagram 287, White plays 1 xh7+ Black replies 1 ... xh7. (Evasion by 1 ... h8 is pointless because of 2 h5.)
items.label: 306A

items.caption: 307A. White moves. The powerful position of his Queen and Bishop suggests the mating pattern of Diagram 284. But White must play the most exact moves. Thus 1 h7+ f8; 2 h8+ would allow Black to escape! The right way: 1 h7+, h8. Black’s King awaits his doom.
items.label: 307A

items.caption: 305B. Black moves. Reluctantly but unavoidably, he defends with 1 ... g6. Reluctantly, because of familiarity with the mating pattern of Diagram 291. But White also knows this mating pattern, and he continues 2 d4, threatening 3 g7 or 3 h8 mate. With so many pieces still on the board, Black cannot prevent the threatened mate. (Remember that his f-Pawn is pinned and paralyzed!)
items.label: 305B

items.caption: 306B. White moves. He follows the pattern: 2 h5+, g8; 3 g5 threatening 4 h7 mate. As 3 ... xg5 would leave him hopelessly behind in material, Black prepares for flight with 3 ... d8. But “there ain’t no hidin’ place.” White winds up with 4 h7+, f8; 5 h8 mate. Another instance of the Queen’s powers.
items.label: 306B

items.caption: 307B. White moves. He has forced Black’s King to a square which is ideal for the hit-and-hold trick. Next comes a discovered check, but there is only one correct one! To wit: 2 g6+! The rest is easy: 2 ... g8; 3 h7+, f8; 4 xf7 mate. (Why did the Bishop go to g6 on the second move?!)
items.label: 307B

items.caption: 308A. White moves. The pattern called for comes from Diagram 295. It is both pretty and picturesque, and has the added attraction of being of practical value. 1 d5+ forces 1 ... h8 (if 1 ... f8 2 f7 mate).
items.label: 308A

items.caption: 308B. White moves. Now comes 2 f7+, g8; 3 h6+ forcing 3 ... h8. Now we are ready for the smothered mate. The sensational 4 g8+! forces 4 ... xg8; and now 5 f7 mate!
items.label: 308B

items.caption: 309A. Black moves. He uses one mating pattern (Diagram 287) to bring about another (Diagram 286). 1 ... g4 threatens 2 ... xh2 mate. White defends with 2 fxg4 (not 2 e1, xh2+; 3 f1, xf2 mate). But after 2 ... hxg4 Black has a new mate threat.
items.label: 309A

items.caption: 310. White moves. His advanced Knight at h5 is a wonderful support for a mating pattern, with the Queen mating at g7. What is the quickest way for White to bring about the mate?
310. White moves. His advanced Knight at h5 is a wonderful support for a mating pattern, with the Queen mating at g7. What is the quickest way for White to bring about the mate?
311. White moves. Working in harmony, his Rook at c3 and his Bishop at e5 can combine to form a mating pattern. How does White use them to force mate in two moves?
312. White moves. His Queen and Bishop are in line to threaten mate at h7; but his own Knight stands in the way of the Bishop. How does White get rid of the Knight, forcing mate in moves?
314A. White moves. His Pawn at c3 is attacked twice, defended only once. White “disregards” the attack because he sees an indirect defense.
items.label: 314A

items.caption: 314A. White moves. His Pawn at c3 is attacked twice, defended only once. White “disregards” the attack because he sees an indirect defense.
items.label: 314A

items.caption: 315A. Black moves. He should retreat his Queen, which is attacked by the White Knight at f3. Instead of retreating, Black plays to win the exchange. He succeeds in this, but loses the game because he fails to look ahead one more move:
items.label: 315A

items.caption: 315B. Black moves. He continues 3 ... xf2 (of course not 3 ... xf2, as his Queen is attacked). Now White plays his ace in the hole: 4 e4! Black’s Queen is trapped, and has no way of returning to safety!
items.label: 315B

items.caption: 316A. White moves. He decides to sacrifice his Bishop at d3 for three Pawns. His idea is to denude the Black King of Pawn protection. White begins with 1 xh7, anticipating 1 ... g6 (leaving the Bishop no retreat); 2 xg6, fxg6; 3 xg6 with a good attack. But Black finds a subtle defense: 1 ... xf3!; 2 gxf3, g6.
items.label: 316A

items.caption: 316A. White moves. He decides to sacrifice his Bishop at d3 for three Pawns. His idea is to denude the Black King of Pawn protection. White begins with 1 xh7, anticipating 1 ... g6 (leaving the Bishop no retreat); 2 xg6, fxg6; 3 xg6 with a good attack. But Black finds a subtle defense: 1 ... xf3!; 2 gxf3, g6.
items.label: 316A

items.caption: 316B. White moves. He proceeds with his plan: 3 xg6, fxg6; 4 xg6? At this instructive moment we can see why Black played 1 ... xf3! For with that move he opened the g-file, with the result that White’s King and Queen are now in line on an open file. A pin is called for: 4 ... g8 pins – and wins – White’s Queen!
items.label: 316B

items.caption: 317B. Black moves. His refutation takes the form of a queening threat: 3 ... c2! 4 d1 is answered by 4 ... cxd1(). 4 c5 is answered by 4 ... xc5. 4 d8 (in order to play 5 c8) is impossible because of 4 ... xd8. The Knight is truly “monarch of all he surveys.”
items.label: 317B

items.caption: 317B. Black moves. His refutation takes the form of a queening threat: 3 ... c2! 4 d1 is answered by 4 ... cxd1(). 4 c5 is answered by 4 ... xc5. 4 d8 (in order to play 5 c8) is impossible because of 4 ... xd8. The Knight is truly “monarch of all he surveys.”
items.label: 317B

items.caption: 318A. White moves. The subtle opening move 1 g1! permits 1 ... xb2?! and White “bites” with 2 xb2!! allowing 2 ... f4+; 3 h2, xd3. Black is a full Queen ahead!
items.label: 318A

items.caption: 319A. Black moves. His Knight is badly out of play, with little prospect of reaching a better post. He sees what looks like a good opportunity of getting rid of the Knight and then regaining the piece by a double attack.
items.label: 319A

items.caption: 319B. Black moves. He must take Bishop or Knight (else he remains a piece down). Whichever way he captures, he opens the d-file. This creates a familiar picture: the pattern for discovered attack! 4 ... dxc3 or 4 ... dxe3 is answered by 5 xh7+, uncovering an attack on the Black Queen. After Black’s King moves, 6 xd8 wins easily. White’s calculations were simple: Black’s moves were forced.
items.label: 319B

items.caption: 319B. Black moves. He must take Bishop or Knight (else he remains a piece down). Whichever way he captures, he opens the d-file. This creates a familiar picture: the pattern for discovered attack! 4 ... dxc3 or 4 ... dxe3 is answered by 5 xh7+, uncovering an attack on the Black Queen. After Black’s King moves, 6 xd8 wins easily. White’s calculations were simple: Black’s moves were forced.
items.label: 319B

items.caption: 320A. Black moves. His Knight attacks White’s Rook at e5. He grabs it by 1 ... xe5? Thus he snatches at the opportunity of winning the exchange, without taking the precaution of trying to discover White’s defense to the threat. White calmly recaptures by 2 dxe5. The new Pawn at e5 menaces the Black Queen, which is sadly hampered by lack of lebensraum. This awkward situation should have been foreseen by Black.
items.label: 320A

items.caption: 321A. White moves. Ostensibly he can win two pieces for a Rook – a clear material gain. Is there a catch? White sees no danger and grabs! After 1 xd5?, xd5; 2 xd5 we have a position which illustrates the most familiar of all familiar themes: the pin!
items.label: 321A

items.caption: 321A. White moves. Ostensibly he can win two pieces for a Rook – a clear material gain. Is there a catch? White sees no danger and grabs! After 1 xd5?, xd5; 2 xd5 we have a position which illustrates the most familiar of all familiar themes: the pin!
items.label: 321A

items.caption: 321B. Black moves. His defense is predicated on the fact that the White Bishop on d6 is pinned and therefore paralyzed. The approved procedure against the pinned piece is, hit it again! 2 ... d8 increases the pressure, forces the win of the Bishop with the exchange ahead.
items.label: 321B

items.caption: 322A. Black moves. What could be more tempting than capturing the Bishop, forking Queen and both Rooks at the same time?! The temptation is irresistible: Black pounces on the Bishop with 1 ... xd3? The reply is electrifying!
items.label: 322A

items.caption: 323A. Black moves. His Queen and Bishop are menaced by a Pawn fork: he must lose a piece. “Counterattack is the best defense,” so: 1 ... d6; 2 fxg5 and now Black swoops down with a powerful check: 2 ... g3+.
items.label: 323A

items.caption: 323A. Black moves. His Queen and Bishop are menaced by a Pawn fork: he must lose a piece. “Counterattack is the best defense,” so: 1 ... d6; 2 fxg5 and now Black swoops down with a powerful check: 2 ... g3+.
items.label: 323A

items.caption: 323B. Black moves. His King is in a bad way. If 3 h1, g7! is decisive (threat: 4 ... h8+). White tries 3 f1, but after 3 ... h3+; 4 e2, g2 mate ends the King’s agony.
items.label: 323B

items.caption: 324A. White moves. He has the pattern for a discovered attack by moving his Knight from c4 and unmasking the action of his Rook on the c-file. The most effective way is (apparently) 1 xe5, attacking Black’s Queen and thereby winning his Knight on g6. But Black coolly allows his Queen to be captured! There follows 1 ... xe5!; 2 xc5.
items.label: 324A

items.caption: 325A. Black moves. He tries an unsound sacrifice in order to penetrate into the heart of the adverse King-side position. He plays 1 ... d5, to open the diagonal leading from his Queen to the hostile King. There follows 2 xg7, xg7; 3 cxd5 and now 3 ... exf4? He hopes for 4 gxf4, xf4+; 5 h1, g3 with good attacking chances.
items.label: 325A

items.caption: 325A. Black moves. He tries an unsound sacrifice in order to penetrate into the heart of the adverse King-side position. He plays 1 ... d5, to open the diagonal leading from his Queen to the hostile King. There follows 2 xg7, xg7; 3 cxd5 and now 3 ... exf4? He hopes for 4 gxf4, xf4+; 5 h1, g3 with good attacking chances.
items.label: 325A

items.caption: 325B. White moves. He defends with a subtle retreating move: 4 f1! Thus he guards the precious Knight’s Pawn, allows his Queen to shift to the threatened zone – and leaves the sacrificed Black Knight dangling with no retreat! Later, at his leisure, White will capture the doomed Knight, with Black bereft of attacking chances. Witty play!
items.label: 325B

items.caption: 326A. White moves. His sacrifice 1 xf7?! is sound if Black accepts it (1 ... xf7; 2 xf7, xf7; 3 xe6, f8; 4 f1+ and wins). But Black defends by refusing the Knight! He plays 1 ... f8 (now he really threatens to capture the Knight), and after 2 e5, xf1+ White is forced to reply 3 xf1 (on 3 xf1 or xf1, xe5 wins a piece).
items.label: 326A

items.caption: 327A. White moves. In this exciting position, he plays 1 xf6, expecting 1 ... gxf6; 2 b1 (threatening 3 h7 mate), f5; 3 b2+ (or 3 h1+) followed by mate. Black therefore defends with 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... g2 mate. Passive defense by White will lose: 2 f1?, xh2 mate. Therefore he continues the attack: 2 c8+!
items.label: 327A

items.caption: 327A. White moves. In this exciting position, he plays 1 xf6, expecting 1 ... gxf6; 2 b1 (threatening 3 h7 mate), f5; 3 b2+ (or 3 h1+) followed by mate. Black therefore defends with 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... g2 mate. Passive defense by White will lose: 2 f1?, xh2 mate. Therefore he continues the attack: 2 c8+!
items.label: 327A

items.caption: 328A. White moves. His combination wins the exchange, but fails to take Black’s resources into account. 1 xa6 is based on the notion that it forces 1 ... bxa6 when 2 xc6 wins a Pawn. Instead Black has the crafty rejoinder 1 ... xa6!; 2 xa6 (this is what Black wants: the removal of the Bishop from e2), bxa6; 3 xc6. White has won the ex change.
items.label: 328A

items.caption: 329A. White moves. The opening thrust 1 f5 is difficult to parry. It strikes again at Black’s pinned Knight and also threatens a “family check” Knight fork at d6. If Black tries 1 ... xf5; 2 xe4, g3 (Knight fork as defense); 3 h7+, g8; 4 4e7 and White remains the exchange ahead. But there is a satisfactory Knight fork defense to the Knight fork threat: 1 ... c4!
items.label: 329A

items.caption: 327B. Black moves. What to do? If he tries flight with 2 ... h7, then 3 b1+ g6; 4 h8 mate. So Black tries the alternative 2 ... xc8; but now he has given up the defense of his h-Pawn, whose other defender is pinned and paralyzed! The sequel: 3 xh6+, g8; 4 xg7 mate. An exciting, fascinating battle of wits!
items.label: 327B

items.caption: 328B. Black moves. He is the exchange down, yet he has a sly move which turns defeat into victory. The move is 3 ... b7!, with a skewer attack on White’s Queen and on the Knight behind the Queen. If now 4 xb7?, xh2+ (discovered attack) wins the Queen. After 4 c3, xf3 (White’s g-Pawn is pinned), Black has two Bishops for a Rook, with an easy win.
items.label: 328B

items.caption: 329B.White moves. His opponent’s amazing unpin prevents the Knight fork at d6 but leaves his Rook at e4 unprotected. However, after 2 xe4, d2+; 3 a1, xe4 Black has regained the Rook by a Knight fork, and in turn prevents White’s Knight fork at d6! A further delightful point: if now 4 e1 (Black’s Knight must not move), c7! as White’s first rank cannot be deserted by 5 xe4??

330A. White moves. He sacrifices a Rook to force a “family check” Knight fork. Yet Black wins, as he has a brilliant defense by means of Knight forks! The play goes 1 h7+?!, xh7!; 2 xf6+, g7! If now (see Diagram 330B) 3 xd5, xe1+ 4 c2 xd4+ winning the Queen and the game by a Knight fork.
items.label: 330A

items.caption: 331A. Black moves. He pushes 1 ... e2, giving his Bishop more scope and threatening to win by 2 ... e3; 3 c4 (if 3 xe3??, xg2 mate), xf3; 4 xd5, f1+ etc. White fights back with 2 xe2. Black presses on the King file with 2 ... e6, threatening 3 ... xe2. White has no additional defense for the Rook at e2, nor can he move it away. Therefore: 3 xe4, fxe4.
items.label: 331A

items.caption: 332A. Black moves. As White’s Queen seems chained to the defense of his g-Pawn (to prevent mate). Black reasons that the Queen is overworked and that 1 ... xd4 is feasible (if 2 xd4??, xg2 mate). Also, if 2 g3, e2 wins quickly. But White, surprisingly enough, plays 2 xf7+, and after 2 ... h8, he seems to have a hopelessly lost game.
items.label: 332A

items.caption: 330B. White moves. He tries 3 xe8+ expecting a King move. But Black, after studying all checks and captures, counters with 3 ... xe8. After 4 xd5 (what else?), he wins artistically with 4 ... xe1+; 5 c2, e3+ followed by 6 ... xd5. A delightful example of resourceful defensive play.
items.label: 330B

items.caption: 331B. White moves. His only defense is counterattack, now that his own Queen and Rook are exposed to double attack. He plays 4 f5, leaving Black in the same predicament, and hoping for the simplifying 4 ... exd3; 5 fxe6 etc. Instead there comes 4 ... exf3! (study every capture!); 5 fxe6 fxg2+ 6 h2 g1() mate! Black looked one move further ahead.
items.label: 331B

items.caption: At first glance, it seems that you have a familiar winning pattern here: double attack. The idea is: you can play 1 xe8 (a move of violence). Then, after 1 ... xe8, you play 2 b5+ followed by 3 xa4 and win.
The pins begin! Black has fianchettoed his Queen’s Bishop so that it will bear down on the long diagonal. He is particularly interested in controlling the vital center square e4.
Now the otherwise desirable 6 e4 cannot be played, for then Black simply replies 6 ... xe4! taking advantage of the pin on White’s Knight at c3.
By means of energetic play, Black has driven the Bishop into a blind alley, gotten rid of the pin, freed his King’s Knight for action and intensified the pin on White’s Queen Knight.

Black now anticipates the following: 10 h3 (to make room for the Bishop), xc3+; 11 bxc3, xg3; 12 fxg3, e7 followed by ... d6, ... d7 and ... 0-0-0. Black would then have a fine game and White’s position would be riddled with Pawn weaknesses.

White’s first aggressive move, curtly changing the picture with kaleidoscopic suddenness. Black’s Bishop at b7 is blocked out of action. Meanwhile Black is menaced with double attack against his Rook at h8 and Knight at e4.
It is generally desirable for Pawns to capture toward the center. In this case, however, 13 hxg3 was out of the question because of the pin by Black’s King Rook.
White’s Knight at c3 has been unpinned, and may come into the game very quickly. Black therefore decides to remove the Knight.
No retreat is necessary! The impertinent Knight cannot be captured, as Black’s f6-Pawn is pinned.
If 19 ... e8; 20 h8+, g8 (or 20 ... e7; 21 xg7+); 21 xf6+ and mate next move. Or 19 ... e8; 20 h5+ d8; 21 h8+ leading to mate.
Still taking advantage of the pin, White forces the King to e7 (removal of the guard), so that 23 xg7+ will be possible. As Black cannot prevent this, he resigns.
Black’s position is somewhat cramped, and the fact that his Knight at c3 is pinned adds to the generally uncomfortable effect.
Wrong! He retreats to threaten a Pawn fork, but the idea is unsound.
The e-Pawn needed support.
11 b5+ also wins, but the text is prettier.

Nimzovich’s procedure here in closing the King file (10 e2!) in order to open it later for a lethal double check and mate, reminds us of the play in Diagram 254A, where Black opened a line of communication in order to close it!

White plans to “fianchetto” his King’s Bishop (play it to g2). As soon as he castles, this Bishop will be guarded by the White King and therefore in a more secure position than the Black Bishop whom he faces on the long diagonal.

Even at this early stage, White has a won game. The d5-Pawn is pinned (why?) and is therefore an immobile target. It is attacked three times and defended three times, but it cannot be guarded by a Pawn (the most secure form of protection).
A neat tactical device makes this move possible despite the fact that the Queen’s Pawn seems to be defended as many times as it is attacked.

What pathetic helplessness! If 14 ... xd5 the Knight fork 15 xe7+ wins a piece. If Black tries to trap the Queen by 14 ... c7 then 15 xa8 (15 xe7+, xe7; 16 xa8 is even simpler), c6; 16 xc6!, xc6; 17 xe7+ still echoes the same theme!
The first point. After the exchange of Bishops, the white squares on the Queen-side become “holes” and vulnerable to occupation by White.

The attack on the weak c-Pawn cannot be parried. Thus 14 ... ac8 allows the same continuation as actually happens in the game; 14 ... d6 allows 15 xe4, dxe4; 16 xc6 and wins; while 14 ... c5 loses by 15 xe4, dxe4; 16 e5 (exploiting the pin), fd8; 17 c6, the Knight Fork winning the exchange.
He must guard the c-Pawn. It is clear that if 15 ... cxd5; 16 xc8+, xc8; 17 xc8+, f8; 18 c1 and White wins easily.

Black resigns, for if 16 ... xc6; 17 e7+ wins the Queen by a Knight fork. If 16 ... xd5; 17 xc8+ wins the Queen by discovered attack. Finally, if 16 ... xc6; 17 xa8+, b8 forced; 18 e5, c8; 19 b7, f8; 20 e7+!, h8; 21 xe4, xe7; 22 g6+ again winning the Queen by discovered attack. Even speedier is 21 xf7+, xf7; 22 c8+ and mate in two more moves (vulnerable first rank).

White’s game is much freer, and his pieces are posted more aggressively. From this it follows that: (a) if new lines are opened, White will benefit accordingly; (b) Black should avoid such line-opening.
So far, so good. Black is momentarily holding his own, for if 11 exf6??, xe2 etc. But White parries cleverly.
Instead of playing 12 cxd4 (which is quite good), White chooses an even sharper method. He now threatens 13 xh7+ or 13 xf7+.
White threatens 16 d5 (blocking the flight of Black’s King) with a quick win.
White could also play h8+, as this move is superfluous.
Stops White’s threat, but the Black King is not happy.
Preventing the skewer check.
White can win in various ways, for example by the Knight fork 23 f6+. But the method he chooses (concentrating on the pin) is certainly the most forthright.
White threatens the Knight fork 25 f6+ followed by 26 xe8, xe8; 27 xe7 with crushing gain of material.
Black resigns, for the pin is beyond endurance; if 25 ... d7; 26 f6 or 26 f6+ wins easily.

With his fourth move, Black “gave up the center” – his center Pawn captured away from the center. The long-range consequence is that White may be able to establish a strong center by playing e4 – now that Black’s Pawn has disappeared from d5.
Black’s pieces do not have access to the center squares. They are therefore likely to be poorly placed. This is particularly true of the Bishop at g6.

If White removes his Queen from attack, his advantage will disappear. For example: 16 d3, h5 saving the Bishop and threatening the double attack ... e2. 16 f3 looks better, but then conies 16 ... h4. (with the mating pattern of Diagrams 307A and 307B); 17 g3, xd4+ followed by 17 ... e5 and again Black has the initiative by coun terattack.
If now 16 ... h5; 17 xh5, xe4; 18 xf7+ h8; 19 f3 retaining a strong initiative.
Still directed against the pinned Knight. The idea is if 17 xh2, h4+ (double attack); 18 g1, xe4 followed by ... h5.

Apparently 17 ... h4 is crushing, but it is defeated by the surprising reply 18 g5! If then 18 ... xe4; 19 xe4, xe4; 20 fxg6, d6; 21 xf7 and wins. Or 18 ... h5; 19 g4 etc. Of course, 18 ... xg5; 19 xg5 is quite hopeless for Black, as he loses too much material.

Decisive! Black cannot play 18 ... f6 (his f-Pawn is pinned). If his Queen moves off the attacking diagonal, 19 fxg6 at last becomes feasible. If 18 ... xg5?; 19 xg5, xe2; 20 xe2 winning Rook and Bishop.
